The more particles in the light's path, the more photons are absorbed: that is the Beer–Lambert law, and it lets you read concentration from how much light is lost.

    c = λνwave relation
    E = hν = hc/λphoton energy
    A = εbcBeer–Lambert
    A = −log(I/I0)absorbance
    The electromagnetic spectrum
    Region—
    Frequency—
    Energy per photon—
    Energy per mole of photons—

    The photoelectric effect
    Photon energy hν—
    Work function Φ—
    Electron kinetic energy—
    Threshold frequency—

    The spectrophotometer
    Absorbance A = εbc—
    Transmittance I/I₀—
    Photons through (measured)—

    Try this

    Predict what will happen first. Then set it up and check.

    1. Where is visible light on the spectrum, and how much energy does one mole of its photons carry?

      What you should see

      Visible light is a thin slice (400–700 nm) in the middle. A mole of 500 nm photons carries about 240 kJ, enough to excite the valence electrons of many molecules, and in the range of the energy of a chemical bond.

    2. Shine light just below the threshold frequency, then just above.

      What you should see

      Below the threshold no electrons come out, no matter how intense the light. Above it electrons are ejected immediately. Turning up the intensity then increases the number of electrons but not their energy: only a higher frequency does that.

    3. Double the concentration of a dye. What happens to the absorbance?

      What you should see

      Absorbance doubles (it is proportional to concentration), but the transmitted light does not halve: it falls exponentially. That is why the graph of A against c is a straight line, and why chemists plot A, not transmittance.

    Worked example

    A violet laser has wavelength 405 nm. Find its frequency, the energy of one photon, and the energy of one mole of photons.

    Try it yourself first, then reveal one step at a time.

    1. Convert the wavelength. 405 nm = 4.05 × 10⁻⁷ m.
    2. Frequency. ν = c/λ = (2.998 × 10⁸ m/s) / (4.05 × 10⁻⁷ m) = 7.40 × 10¹⁴ Hz.
    3. Energy of one photon. E = hν = (6.626 × 10⁻³⁴ J·s)(7.40 × 10¹⁴ s⁻¹) = 4.90 × 10⁻¹⁹ J.
    4. Energy of a mole. (4.90 × 10⁻¹⁹ J)(6.022 × 10²³ mol⁻¹) = 2.95 × 10⁵ J/mol = 295 kJ/mol.

    Common mistakes

    • Forgetting to convert nanometers to meters before using c = λν.
    • Thinking brighter light ejects faster electrons. Intensity controls how many; frequency controls how energetic.
    • Thinking longer wavelength means higher energy. Energy is inversely proportional to wavelength.
    • Plotting transmittance against concentration and expecting a line. Absorbance is the one that is linear.
    • Choosing the wrong wavelength for a measurement. Use the wavelength where the sample absorbs most (the color complementary to what you see).

    Why this matters in chemistry

    A spectrophotometer measures absorbance at one wavelength. You prepare solutions of known concentration, measure their absorbance, and draw a calibration line (A against c); the slope is εb. Then you measure an unknown and read its concentration off the line. The law fails at high concentration, where particles interact or too little light gets through, so keep absorbances under about 1.

    The photoelectric effect (no electrons below a threshold frequency) was what convinced physicists that light comes in packets: if light were just a wave, enough intensity should eventually free electrons at any frequency. The same idea gives photoelectron spectroscopy, where the measured electron energies reveal binding energies.

    Check yourself: which photon has the most energy?

    AP Unit 3

    Separating mixtures

    A mixture can be taken apart without any chemical reaction, by using a physical property in which the parts differ: size, attraction to a surface, or boiling point.

    The idea

    Pure substances keep their identity in a mixture, so they keep their different properties, and those differences are handles for separating them. Sand and water differ in particle size: pour through a filter. Salt and water differ in volatility: evaporate the water. Dyes in ink differ in how strongly they stick to paper compared with how strongly they dissolve in a solvent: use chromatography. Two liquids with different boiling points: use distillation.

    In chromatography a solvent (the mobile phase) creeps up paper (the stationary phase) and carries each dye along. Dyes that attract the paper strongly are held back; dyes that prefer the solvent race ahead. In distillation, the more volatile liquid (the one with the weaker intermolecular forces) escapes as vapor more readily, so the vapor is richer in it.

    Paper chromatography

    The paper is polar (cellulose). Polar dyes stick to it; nonpolar dyes prefer the solvent. A more polar solvent drags the polar dyes further. Rf = distance the spot moved ÷ distance the solvent front moved.

    Distillation
    Boiling temperature—
    Ethanol in the pot—
    Ethanol in the vapor now—
    Ethanol in the distillate—

    Model: an ideal solution (Raoult's law) of ethanol (boils at 78.4 °C) and water (100 °C). Real ethanol–water mixtures form an azeotrope near 96% ethanol by mass, so distillation alone can't go further.

    Try this

    Predict what will happen first. Then set it up and check.

    1. Run the marker-ink chromatogram. Which dye travels furthest?

      What you should see

      The least polar dye (yellow) is attracted least to the polar paper and travels furthest (highest Rf); the most polar (blue) is held back. A mixture appearing as one color separates into its dyes.

    2. Change the solvent to a more polar one and run again.

      What you should see

      Every dye moves further: the polar solvent competes better with the paper for the polar dyes. Rf values change with the solvent, so they are only comparable under the same conditions.

    3. Distill a 50:50 ethanol–water mixture. What is in the receiver first?

      What you should see

      The first drops are about 70% ethanol (the vapor is richer in the lower-boiling liquid). As ethanol leaves, the pot gets richer in water, so the boiling temperature climbs toward 100 °C.

    Worked example

    On a chromatogram the solvent front moved 8.0 cm. Spots: yellow at 6.8 cm, red at 4.6 cm, blue at 1.2 cm. Find the Rf of each dye, and say which is the most polar.

    Try it yourself first, then reveal one step at a time.

    1. Definition. Rf = (distance traveled by the spot) / (distance traveled by the solvent front), measured from the starting line.
    2. Calculate. Yellow: 6.8/8.0 = 0.85. Red: 4.6/8.0 = 0.58. Blue: 1.2/8.0 = 0.15.
    3. Interpret. The smallest Rf belongs to the dye most strongly attracted to the polar paper: blue is the most polar, and yellow is the least.

    Common mistakes

    • Measuring Rf from the bottom of the paper instead of from the starting line.
    • Using a pen (ink dissolves in the solvent) for the starting line: use pencil.
    • Saying the more volatile liquid is the one with the stronger intermolecular forces. It has the weaker ones, and the lower boiling point.
    • Expecting simple distillation to give a perfectly pure product from liquids with close boiling points.
    • Calling separation a chemical change. No new substances form; only physical properties are used.

    Choosing a method

    Filtration separates an insoluble solid from a liquid (different particle sizes). Evaporation or crystallization recovers a dissolved solid. Distillation separates liquids by boiling point. Chromatography separates small amounts of similar substances by how they divide between a stationary and a mobile phase: in paper or thin-layer chromatography, the stationary phase is polar; in column chromatography it can be a packed solid, and substances elute in order of their attraction to it.

    The same principle, differences in intermolecular attractions, runs through all of them: stronger attraction to the stationary phase means moving more slowly; weaker attractions between molecules means boiling more easily.

    Check yourself: which method best separates the colored dyes in black ink?

    AP Unit 4

    Balancing equations

    A chemical reaction rearranges atoms; it never makes or destroys them. Balancing an equation is just making sure every atom you start with shows up in the products.

    The idea

    Think of building models from a pile of identical bricks. If you take apart two toy cars and build one airplane, every brick must end up somewhere. A balanced equation is the parts list: the same number of each kind of atom on both sides.

    You balance by changing the coefficients (the numbers in front of formulas), never the subscripts. Changing a subscript changes the substance: H₂O₂ is hydrogen peroxide, not water. A coefficient only changes how many of that molecule take part.

    Balance it, then react

    Try this

    Predict what will happen first. Then set it up and check.

    1. Balance hydrogen burning in oxygen: H₂ + O₂ → H₂O. Start by counting oxygen atoms.

      What you should see

      With 1 O₂ there are two O atoms on the left but only one in a single H₂O. Put a 2 in front of H₂O to fix the oxygen, which makes four H on the right; then a 2 in front of H₂. Result: 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O.

    2. Try to "balance" by changing a subscript. What does the particle picture say?

      What you should see

      You can only change coefficients here, and for good reason: H₂O₂ would be a different molecule. Subscripts are part of a substance's identity.

    3. Balance the combustion of ethene, C₂H₄ + O₂ → CO₂ + H₂O. Balance C and H first, oxygen last.

      What you should see

      2 CO₂ for the 2 carbons, 2 H₂O for the 4 hydrogens: that makes 4 + 2 = 6 oxygen atoms on the right, so 3 O₂ on the left. C₂H₄ + 3O₂ → 2CO₂ + 2H₂O.

    Worked example

    Balance: C₃H₈ + O₂ → CO₂ + H₂O.

    Try it yourself first, then reveal one step at a time.

    1. List the atoms. Left: 3 C, 8 H, 2 O. Right: 1 C, 2 H, 3 O.
    2. Balance the carbon. Three carbons on the left, so 3 CO₂ on the right.
    3. Balance the hydrogen. Eight H on the left, so 4 H₂O on the right (4 × 2 = 8).
    4. Balance the oxygen last. Right side: 3 × 2 + 4 = 10 O atoms. O₂ comes in pairs, so 5 O₂ on the left.
    5. Check. C₃H₈ + 5O₂ → 3CO₂ + 4H₂O: C 3 = 3, H 8 = 8, O 10 = 10. ✓ The coefficients 1, 5, 3, 4 have no common factor, so this is the simplest whole-number set.

    Common mistakes

    • Changing subscripts instead of coefficients. That changes the substance.
    • Forgetting to multiply a coefficient through a whole formula, including atoms inside parentheses: 3Ca(OH)₂ has 3 Ca, 6 O and 6 H.
    • Balancing oxygen first in a combustion. It appears in two products; do it last.
    • Leaving fractions or non-simplest coefficients. Multiply through to clear a fraction; divide out common factors.
    • Thinking the equation shows how fast or whether a reaction happens. It only keeps the atom book.

    Strategy

    Balance the atoms that appear in the fewest formulas first, and leave elements that appear alone (like O₂ or H₂) until the end, because you can change their coefficient without disturbing anything else. If you hit a snag with an odd number on one side, double everything you've done and try again. Check at the end by counting each atom on both sides, and for ionic equations, by also checking that the total charge is the same on both sides.

    The coefficients are also mole ratios: in 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O, 2 mol of H₂ react with 1 mol of O₂ to make 2 mol of water. That is the first step of every stoichiometry problem.

    Types of reactions and physical vs chemical change

    A chemical change makes new substances (bonds break and form); a physical change (melting, boiling, dissolving, mixing) changes only the arrangement or phase, and the substance keeps its identity. Common reaction types: synthesis (A + B → AB), decomposition (AB → A + B), single replacement (A + BC → AC + B, a redox reaction), double replacement (AB + CD → AD + CB; precipitation and acid–base reactions), combustion (a fuel plus O₂ gives CO₂ and H₂O), and acid–base reactions (a proton transfer). Many are also redox reactions whenever oxidation numbers change.

    Check yourself: in the balanced equation __Al + __O₂ → __Al₂O₃, what is the coefficient of O₂?

    AP Unit 4

    Stoichiometry & limiting reagent

    A balanced equation is a recipe. Stoichiometry scales the recipe to the amounts you actually have, and tells you what runs out first.

    The idea

    To make a sandwich you need 2 slices of bread and 1 slice of cheese. With 10 slices of bread and 3 slices of cheese you can make only 3 sandwiches: the cheese runs out first. Bread is left over. In a reaction the same thing happens: the limiting reagent is used up first and decides how much product forms. The other reactant is in excess and some is left over.

    The recipe is the balanced equation, and its coefficients are mole ratios. You can't compare grams directly (a gram of H₂ is a lot more molecules than a gram of O₂), so every stoichiometry problem passes through moles.

    Assumption upgrade

    Before
    we assumed 100% yield and exactly the right amount of each reactant
    So we didn't need
    to ask which reactant runs out, or how much product we really get
    Now
    real reactions use uneven amounts and lose some product
    So we need
    the limiting reagent (it sets the theoretical yield) and the percent yield
    grams → moles → mole ratio → moles → gramsthe stoichiometry road
    % yield = actual / theoretical × 100real versus ideal
    Run the reaction
    Limiting reagent—
    Left over—
    Theoretical yield—
    Actual yield—

    Each particle in the picture stands for 0.5 mol, so the table can show real masses.

    Try this

    Predict what will happen first. Then set it up and check.

    1. Make ammonia with 4 N₂ and 6 H₂. Which runs out?

      What you should see

      The recipe needs 3 H₂ for every N₂. Six H₂ can only handle 2 N₂, so H₂ is limiting: it makes 4 NH₃, and 2 N₂ are left over.

    2. Give exactly the recipe amounts: 4 N₂ and 12 H₂.

      What you should see

      Both run out at the same time: a stoichiometric mixture, with nothing left over and 8 NH₃ made.

    3. Now lose some product: set the percent yield to 75%.

      What you should see

      The theoretical yield is still 8 NH₃ (all the limiting reagent reacts on paper), but only 6 appear: the actual yield is 75% of the theoretical.

    Worked example

    10.0 g of N₂ reacts with 3.00 g of H₂ in N₂ + 3H₂ → 2NH₃. Find the limiting reagent, the theoretical yield of NH₃, and the mass of excess reactant left over.

    Try it yourself first, then reveal one step at a time.

    1. Convert to moles. N₂: 10.0 g ÷ 28.02 g/mol = 0.357 mol. H₂: 3.00 g ÷ 2.016 g/mol = 1.49 mol.
    2. Find the limiting reagent. N₂ needs 3 mol H₂ per mol: 0.357 × 3 = 1.07 mol H₂ is needed, and 1.49 mol is available, so H₂ is in excess and N₂ is limiting.
    3. Theoretical yield. 0.357 mol N₂ × (2 mol NH₃ / 1 mol N₂) = 0.714 mol NH₃; × 17.03 g/mol = 12.2 g NH₃.
    4. Excess left over. H₂ used = 1.07 mol; left = 1.49 − 1.07 = 0.42 mol × 2.016 g/mol = 0.85 g H₂.

    Common mistakes

    • Comparing grams of reactants to choose the limiting reagent. Convert to moles and use the coefficients.
    • Using the coefficients on grams instead of moles.
    • Basing the yield on the excess reactant. The limiting reagent controls how much can form.
    • Calling the actual yield the "theoretical yield". Theoretical is the calculated maximum; actual is what you measured.
    • Forgetting to use the balanced equation (e.g. using 1:1 when the ratio is 1:3).

    Two ways to find the limiting reagent

    Compare moles to coefficients: divide each reactant's moles by its coefficient; the smaller number belongs to the limiting reagent. For 0.357 mol N₂ (coefficient 1) and 1.49 mol H₂ (coefficient 3): 0.357 against 0.497, so N₂ is limiting. Compare yields: calculate how much product each reactant could make; the smaller amount is the real theoretical yield.

    Percent yield compares what you got to what the limiting reagent could have given. It is always at most 100% in a clean experiment; a value above 100% usually means the product still contains water or another impurity.

    Check yourself: 4Al + 3O₂ → 2Al₂O₃. You mix 4.0 mol Al with 4.0 mol O₂. Which is limiting?

    AP Unit 4

    Net ionic equations & precipitation

    Mix two clear solutions and sometimes a solid appears. The solid forms because two particular ions find each other and lock together; every other ion just watches.

    The idea

    Ionic compounds that dissolve in water exist as separate, moving ions. When two such solutions are mixed, every positive ion meets every negative ion. Most of these partners prefer to stay dissolved (they are soluble). But if one cation–anion pair forms an insoluble compound, the pair clumps into a solid that falls out of the solution: a precipitate.

    The ions that never take part, floating along unchanged, are spectator ions. A net ionic equation deletes the spectators and shows only what actually happens. To predict whether a precipitate forms, swap the partners and check the solubility rules for each new compound.

    Mix two solutions
    Precipitate—
    Spectator ions—

    Spectator ions are crossed out in the complete ionic equation. Solubility rules are on the Reference sheet (Solubility & ions tab).

    Try this

    Predict what will happen first. Then set it up and check.

    1. Mix silver nitrate with sodium chloride. Which ions clump?

      What you should see

      Ag⁺ and Cl⁻ stick together as white AgCl and sink. Na⁺ and NO₃⁻ stay dissolved: they are the spectators. Net ionic equation: Ag⁺(aq) + Cl⁻(aq) → AgCl(s).

    2. Now mix sodium chloride with potassium nitrate.

      What you should see

      Nothing happens: every possible pair (NaNO₃, KCl) is soluble, so all four ions are spectators and there is no net ionic equation. Mixing is not the same as reacting.

    3. Mix lead(II) nitrate with potassium iodide. Why is the net equation different in form?

      What you should see

      The yellow solid PbI₂ needs two iodide ions per lead ion: Pb²⁺ + 2I⁻ → PbI₂(s). The charges of the ions set the formula, and the subscript becomes the coefficient in the net ionic equation.

    Worked example

    Write the net ionic equation for mixing aqueous BaCl₂ and Na₂SO₄.

    Try it yourself first, then reveal one step at a time.

    1. Dissociate. BaCl₂ → Ba²⁺ + 2Cl⁻. Na₂SO₄ → 2Na⁺ + SO₄²⁻.
    2. Swap partners. Possible products: BaSO₄ and NaCl.
    3. Check solubility. NaCl is soluble (all Na⁺ salts are). BaSO₄ is insoluble (sulfates are soluble except with Ba²⁺, Sr²⁺, Pb²⁺).
    4. Complete ionic equation. Ba²⁺ + 2Cl⁻ + 2Na⁺ + SO₄²⁻ → BaSO₄(s) + 2Na⁺ + 2Cl⁻.
    5. Cancel spectators (Na⁺ and Cl⁻): Ba²⁺(aq) + SO₄²⁻(aq) → BaSO₄(s). Check: charge 0 on both sides. ✓

    Common mistakes

    • Writing a precipitate as separate ions. A solid is written as the whole formula, with (s).
    • Splitting a solid, a gas or a weak electrolyte into ions in the complete ionic equation. Only soluble ionic compounds (aq) are split.
    • Forgetting to check both new compounds. Only one needs to be insoluble for a reaction, but you must check both.
    • Forgetting that the net ionic equation must balance in charge as well as in atoms.
    • Saying a spectator ion "does nothing". It still carries charge and keeps the solution neutral, but it is not changed.

    Three kinds of equation

    The molecular equation writes every compound as a whole formula: AgNO₃(aq) + NaCl(aq) → AgCl(s) + NaNO₃(aq). The complete ionic equation splits every soluble ionic compound into its ions and leaves solids whole. The net ionic equation removes the spectators. All three are balanced, but the net ionic equation tells the real chemical story, and it is the one used for stoichiometry: the amount of precipitate depends only on the amount of the limiting ion.

    Precipitation is used to remove ions from water (for example, hydroxide or sulfide precipitates remove heavy metals) and to detect them (a white precipitate with silver nitrate indicates chloride).

    Check yourself: Pb(NO₃)₂(aq) is mixed with NaCl(aq). What is the net ionic equation?

    AP Unit 4

    Oxidation states & redox

    In a redox reaction, electrons move from one species to another. Oxidation numbers are the bookkeeping that tells you who gave and who took.

    The idea

    Drop a strip of zinc into blue copper(II) sulfate solution. The zinc dissolves and a red-brown crust of copper appears on it, and the blue fades. Zinc atoms are handing electrons to copper ions. The one that loses electrons is oxidized; the one that gains electrons is reduced. The mnemonic: OIL RIG, Oxidation Is Loss, Reduction Is Gain (of electrons).

    Oxidation and reduction always go together, because electrons can't vanish. The substance that gets oxidized is the reducing agent (it reduces the other one); the substance that gets reduced is the oxidizing agent. To follow electrons in molecules, where nothing is cleanly lost or gained, we assign oxidation numbers, the charge an atom would have if every bond were completely ionic.

    Watch the electrons move
    Oxidized (loses e⁻)—
    Reduced (gains e⁻)—
    Reducing agent—
    Oxidizing agent—
    Find the oxidation number

    Try this

    Predict what will happen first. Then set it up and check.

    1. Zinc in copper(II) solution. Which loses electrons?

      What you should see

      Zn goes from 0 to +2: oxidized (it is the reducing agent). Cu²⁺ goes from +2 to 0: reduced (the oxidizing agent). Each zinc atom releases 2 electrons that one Cu²⁺ ion picks up.

    2. Copper in silver nitrate: why two silver ions for each copper atom?

      What you should see

      Each Cu atom gives up 2 electrons, but each Ag⁺ can accept only 1. So two Ag⁺ are reduced for each Cu oxidized: electrons lost must equal electrons gained.

    3. Find the oxidation number of manganese in KMnO₄.

      What you should see

      K is +1 (group 1) and O is −2 (4 oxygens: −8). The compound is neutral, so +1 + x − 8 = 0 and Mn is +7. That unusually high number is why permanganate is such a strong oxidizing agent.

    Worked example

    In the reaction 2Al + 3Cl₂ → 2AlCl₃, identify what is oxidized and reduced, the oxidizing and reducing agents, and the number of electrons transferred.

    Try it yourself first, then reveal one step at a time.

    1. Assign oxidation numbers. Elements on their own are 0: Al = 0 and Cl₂ = 0. In AlCl₃, Cl is −1 (it is more electronegative), so Al is +3.
    2. See what changed. Al: 0 → +3 (increase: oxidized). Cl: 0 → −1 (decrease: reduced).
    3. Name the agents. The oxidized species, Al, is the reducing agent. The reduced species, Cl₂, is the oxidizing agent.
    4. Count the electrons. 2 Al atoms lose 3 e⁻ each: 6 e⁻. 3 Cl₂ is 6 Cl atoms, each gaining 1: 6 e⁻. They match. 6 electrons are transferred.

    Common mistakes

    • Mixing up which is which: the substance that is oxidized is the reducing agent, not the oxidizing agent.
    • Treating oxidation numbers as real charges in covalent compounds. In CO₂ carbon is +4 by convention, not a C⁴⁺ ion.
    • Forgetting the exceptions: H is −1 in metal hydrides (NaH), O is −1 in peroxides (H₂O₂).
    • Forgetting that the oxidation numbers in a polyatomic ion sum to its charge, not to zero.
    • Thinking only reactions with oxygen are oxidations. Oxidation is loss of electrons, with or without oxygen.

    Rules for assigning oxidation numbers

    (1) An atom in a pure element is 0. (2) A monatomic ion has its charge. (3) The numbers in a neutral compound add to 0; in an ion they add to its charge. (4) Group 1 metals are +1, group 2 metals +2. (5) Fluorine is −1. (6) Hydrogen is +1 (−1 with metals); oxygen is −2 (−1 in peroxides). (7) Other halogens are −1 unless combined with oxygen or fluorine. Use the rules in this order of priority; the one unknown atom gets whatever makes the sum right.

    A reaction is a redox reaction if any oxidation number changes. Combustion, corrosion, batteries, respiration and bleaching are all redox processes.

    Check yourself: in 2Na + Cl₂ → 2NaCl, what is the oxidizing agent?

    AP Unit 5

    Reaction rates & rate laws

    How fast does a reaction go, and what does the speed depend on? The rate law is the recipe that answers it.

    The idea

    A reaction rate is how quickly reactants disappear or products appear: change in concentration per second. Think of a busy dance floor where pairs must bump into each other to react. Crowd the floor and bumps happen far more often. Whether the rate doubles, quadruples or doesn't change when you double a concentration tells you the order with respect to that reactant.

    A rate law has the form rate = k[A]m[B]n. The exponents m and n are the orders and must be found from experiments, not read from the balanced equation. The constant k is the rate constant: bigger k, faster reaction at the same concentrations.

    Assumption upgrade Before, a balanced equation told us how much reacts. We assumed it also told us how fast. It doesn't: the coefficients give amounts, but the orders in the rate law come from experiment.
    Particles reacting
    A left—
    Products formed—
    Reactions in last 4 s—
    Rate law—
    Initial-rates detective

    Compare two trials where only one concentration changes. By what factor did the rate change?

    Try this

    Predict first, then watch the counts and the reaction count.

    1. First order: double the number of A particles. Does the reaction rate double?

      What you should see

      About twice as many reactions per second at 60 particles as at 30. Each A reacts on its own, so more A means proportionally more reactions: rate = k[A].

    2. Second order: do the same experiment. What happens now?

      What you should see

      Doubling A roughly quadruples the reactions per second, because every A can bump into twice as many partners and there are twice as many A. Rate = k[A]².

    3. Use the detective: find a pair of trials where only [B] changes.

      What you should see

      Divide the rates of those two trials, then ask: what power of the concentration ratio gives that factor? Ratio 1 means order 0, ratio equal to the concentration ratio means 1, its square means 2.

    Worked example

    Experiments for A + B → products: Trial 1: [A] = 0.10 M, [B] = 0.10 M, rate = 2.0×10⁻³ M/s. Trial 2: [A] = 0.20, [B] = 0.10, rate = 8.0×10⁻³. Trial 3: [A] = 0.10, [B] = 0.30, rate = 6.0×10⁻³. Find the rate law and k.

    Try it yourself first, then reveal one step at a time.

    1. Order in A. Compare trials 1 and 2: only [A] changed, by a factor 2. The rate rose by 8.0/2.0 = 4. Since 2m = 4, m = 2.
    2. Order in B. Compare trials 1 and 3: only [B] changed, by a factor 3. The rate rose 6.0/2.0 = 3, and 3n = 3, so n = 1.
    3. Write the rate law. rate = k[A]²[B].
    4. Solve for k with any trial: k = rate / ([A]²[B]) = (2.0×10⁻³) / (0.10² × 0.10) = 2.0 M⁻²s⁻¹. The units come out of making M/s on the left: M⁻² s⁻¹ × M³ = M/s.

    Common mistakes

    • Using the coefficients in the balanced equation as the orders. Only a (one-step) elementary reaction works that way.
    • Comparing two trials where more than one concentration changed. Change one at a time, or untangle the factors carefully.
    • Forgetting that k depends on temperature: a different temperature means a different k.
    • Dropping the units of k. They depend on the overall order: M/s for zero order, s⁻¹ for first, M⁻¹s⁻¹ for second.
    • Zero order does not mean zero rate. It means the rate doesn't depend on that concentration.

    Units of k

    Rate has units M/s. For overall order N, k has units M1−N·s⁻¹: zero order M/s, first order s⁻¹, second order M⁻¹s⁻¹, third order M⁻²s⁻¹. You can read the overall order straight from the units of k.

    Check yourself: tripling [A] makes the rate 9 times as fast. What is the order in A?

    AP Unit 5

    Integrated rate laws & half-life

    Rate laws tell you how fast. Integrated rate laws tell you how much is left after a given time, and which graph turns into a straight line.

    The idea

    Watch a jar of reactant disappear. A zero-order reaction loses the same amount every second, like a tap emptying a bucket at a steady rate. A first-order reaction loses the same fraction every second, like a bank balance shrinking by 10% a day: fast at first, then slower. A second-order reaction slows down even more as it goes, because the reactants meet less and less often.

    Each order has one graph that comes out as a straight line: [A] vs t (zero), ln[A] vs t (first), 1/[A] vs t (second). If you measure concentrations over time, the straight one tells you the order. The half-life is the time for [A] to fall to half. For first order it never changes, however much you start with. That is the signature of exponential decay.

    Assumption upgrade Before, the rate law gave the rate at one instant, so we only needed concentrations at that instant. Now we want the concentration at a later time, so we need the integrated forms, and time enters the equations.
    Zero order[A] = [A]₀ − ktt½ = [A]₀ / 2k
    First orderln[A] = ln[A]₀ − ktt½ = 0.693 / k
    Second order1/[A] = 1/[A]₀ + ktt½ = 1 / (k[A]₀)
    Watch it decay
    [A] now—
    Half-life—
    Fraction left—
    Straight-line graph—
    Mystery data: which order?

    Which of the three graphs is a straight line? Its order is the answer.

    Try this

    Predict first, then check on the graphs.

    1. First order: play to 100 s and watch the jar. Is the second half-life the same length as the first?

      What you should see

      Yes: each half-life takes the same time. At t½ half is left, at 2t½ a quarter, at 3t½ an eighth. Only first order behaves like this.

    2. Zero order: does it ever run out?

      What you should see

      Yes. It loses a fixed amount per second, so it hits zero at a definite time, [A]₀/k. First and second order only approach zero.

    3. Second order: look at the 1/[A] graph.

      What you should see

      The 1/[A] graph is a straight line rising with slope k. The other two curve.

    Worked example

    The decomposition of N₂O₅ is first order with k = 5.0×10⁻⁴ s⁻¹. Starting with 0.800 M, how much is left after 20.0 minutes, and what is the half-life?

    Try it yourself first, then reveal one step at a time.

    1. Pick the equation. First order, and we want a concentration at a time: ln[A] = ln[A]₀ − kt.
    2. Convert time to seconds so it matches k: 20.0 min × 60 = 1200 s.
    3. Compute kt. kt = (5.0×10⁻⁴)(1200) = 0.60. Then [A] = [A]₀·e−kt = 0.800 × e−0.60 = 0.800 × 0.549 = 0.439 M.
    4. Half-life. t½ = 0.693 / k = 0.693 / 5.0×10⁻⁴ = 1.4×10³ s (about 23 min). Check: 1200 s is a bit less than one half-life, so a bit more than half should be left. 0.439/0.800 = 55%. ✓

    Common mistakes

    • Using minutes with a k in s⁻¹. Convert time first.
    • Using the first-order half-life formula for a second-order reaction. Only first order has a constant half-life, 0.693/k.
    • Forgetting the sign: the slope of ln[A] vs t is −k, so k itself is positive.
    • Using log base 10 where the equation needs ln.
    • Thinking a half-life means the reaction is "half done" at a fixed time regardless of order. In second order, each successive half-life is longer; in zero order, shorter.

    Why first order is a straight ln plot

    If the rate is proportional to [A], the amount lost each second is a fixed fraction of what is there, and the solution is exponential: [A] = [A]₀e−kt. Taking ln of both sides gives ln[A] = ln[A]₀ − kt, a straight line with slope −k. Second order and zero order integrate the same way and give their own lines.

    Check yourself: a first-order reaction has t½ = 40 s. What percent of A is left after 80 s?

    AP Unit 5

    Collision theory, activation energy & catalysts

    Why does heating speed a reaction up, and how can a catalyst do it without heat? The answer is a hill and a crowd of particles.

    The idea

    For particles to react they must collide, hard enough and facing the right way. Think of pushing a ball over a hill: only a ball with enough energy gets to the other side. The height of that hill is the activation energy, Ea. Most collisions are too gentle and the particles just bounce apart.

    At any temperature, particles have a spread of energies (the Boltzmann distribution). Raising the temperature does two things, but the big one is that it stretches the high-energy tail, so many more collisions clear the hill. A catalyst doesn't heat anything: it offers a different path with a lower hill, so a much larger share of ordinary collisions succeed. It is not used up and doesn't change the overall ΔE.

    Assumption upgrade Before, we assumed that every collision between reactants makes products, so we only needed to count collisions. Now we also need enough energy and the right orientation, so only a small fraction of collisions are effective.
    Energy distribution & collisions
    Effective Eₐ—
    Collisions above Eₐ—
    Rate vs 300 K, no catalyst, same Eₐ—
    Reactions so far—

    The box is not to scale: it uses a scaled-down hill so you can see reactions happen. The graph and numbers are real.

    The energy hill
    Forward Eₐ—
    Reverse Eₐ—
    ΔH (unchanged by a catalyst)—
    Type—

    Try this

    Predict, then look at both the box and the graph.

    1. Heat the gas by 100 K. By roughly what factor does the number of high-energy collisions change?

      What you should see

      The tail above Eₐ grows by a factor of tens to thousands for a typical Eₐ, while the average energy rises only a third. That is why a 10 K rise can double a rate.

    2. Add a catalyst at 300 K. Compare with heating.

      What you should see

      The temperature (and the curve) hasn't changed, but the Eₐ marker moved left into a much fatter part of the distribution. The fraction of effective collisions rose by many orders of magnitude.

    3. On the energy hill, add the catalyst. Does ΔH change?

      What you should see

      The barrier shrinks for both directions, but reactants and products stay at the same heights. ΔH is the same; only the speed changes.

    Worked example

    A reaction has Ea = 75 kJ/mol. By what factor does its rate constant increase when T rises from 300 K to 310 K? (R = 8.314 J/mol·K)

    Try it yourself first, then reveal one step at a time.

    1. Use the Arrhenius form for two temperatures. ln(k₂/k₁) = (Ea/R)(1/T₁ − 1/T₂).
    2. Convert units. Ea = 75 000 J/mol so it matches R in J.
    3. Compute. 1/300 − 1/310 = 1.075×10⁻⁴ K⁻¹. Ea/R = 75000/8.314 = 9.02×10³ K. The product is 0.970.
    4. Exponentiate. k₂/k₁ = e0.970 = 2.6. A 10 K rise multiplies the rate by about 2.6, the old "doubles every 10 °C" rule of thumb (it depends on Eₐ).

    Common mistakes

    • Thinking a catalyst supplies energy or changes ΔH. It lowers Eₐ for both the forward and reverse reactions equally.
    • Saying heat makes every particle go faster by the same amount. Temperature widens the whole distribution; the tail grows most.
    • Forgetting to convert Eₐ from kJ to J, or to use Kelvin, in the Arrhenius equation.
    • Saying a catalyst is a reactant. It is consumed in one step and regenerated in another, so it doesn't appear in the net equation.
    • Treating "more collisions" as the whole story. Most of the speed-up from heating comes from more energetic collisions, not more frequent ones.

    The Arrhenius equation

    The rate constant is k = A·e−Ea/RT. The factor A bundles collision frequency and orientation. The exponential factor is roughly the fraction of collisions with energy of at least Ea. A plot of ln k against 1/T is a straight line with slope −Ea/R.

    Types of catalysts

    A homogeneous catalyst is in the same phase as the reactants (aqueous I⁻ catalyzing H₂O₂ decomposition; Cl radicals in the atmosphere). A heterogeneous catalyst is in a different phase, usually a solid surface: reactant molecules adsorb onto the metal, their bonds weaken, they react, and the products leave (a catalytic converter's Pt/Pd/Rh; iron in the Haber process). Enzymes are biological catalysts: a substrate binds to the enzyme's active site, which holds it in the right orientation and stabilizes the transition state. All catalysts lower the activation energy by providing a different mechanism; none changes ΔH or the equilibrium position.

    Check yourself: what does a catalyst change?

    AP Unit 5

    Reaction mechanisms

    Most reactions don't happen in one step. A mechanism is the movie of what really happens, and the slowest scene sets the speed.

    The idea

    Imagine a busy sandwich shop: one person slices bread (fast), one adds fillings (fast), and one wraps each sandwich, slowly. However fast the first two work, orders go out at the speed of the wrapper. In a reaction, that slow stage is the rate-determining step, and it's the step with the highest energy hill.

    A mechanism is a list of elementary steps: single collisions or breakups. For an elementary step, and only for those, the rate law comes straight from the coefficients: A + B → C has rate = k[A][B]. Species made in one step and used up in a later one are intermediates: they never appear in the overall equation, and they can't appear in the final rate law. A catalyst is the reverse: used first, then regenerated.

    Assumption upgrade Before, we assumed a balanced equation was a single event, so its coefficients could set the rate. Now we know the equation is only the sum of several steps, so the rate law must come from the slow step.
    Walk through a mechanism

    Tap the hill you think is the rate-determining step.

    Write the rate law
      Rate law?
      Overall order?
      Label every species

      Tap a species to cycle: reactant, product, intermediate, catalyst. Then press Check.

      Try this

      Predict first, then use the labs above.

      1. Pick the NO₂ + CO reaction. Which species is in the net equation's reactants but is not in the rate law?

        What you should see

        CO. The rate law is rate = k[NO₂]²: CO takes part only in the fast second step, after the slow one, so changing [CO] doesn't change the speed.

      2. Pick H₂O₂ + I⁻. Why does iodide appear in the rate law but not in the overall equation?

        What you should see

        I⁻ is a catalyst: it reacts in the slow step (so it affects the rate) and is regenerated in the fast step (so it cancels in the net equation).

      3. Pick 2NO + O₂ and step through the rate law. What do we do with N₂O₂?

        What you should see

        The slow step contains an intermediate, so we replace [N₂O₂] using the fast equilibrium before it: forward rate = reverse rate gives [N₂O₂] ∝ [NO]².

      Worked example

      Proposed mechanism: Step 1 (slow): A + B → C + D. Step 2 (fast): C + B → E. Find the overall reaction, the intermediate and the rate law.

      Try it yourself first, then reveal one step at a time.

      1. Add the steps. A + B + C + B → C + D + E. Cancel what appears on both sides (C): A + 2B → D + E.
      2. Find the intermediate. C is produced in step 1 and consumed in step 2, and isn't in the overall reaction. C is the intermediate.
      3. Find the slow step. Step 1 is slow, so it sets the rate.
      4. Write its rate law. Step 1 is elementary, so rate = k[A][B]. It has no intermediate on the left, so this is the answer. Note it is not k[A][B]², even though the overall reaction uses 2B.

      Common mistakes

      • Using the overall equation's coefficients for the rate law. Only an elementary step works that way.
      • Leaving an intermediate in the rate law. Express it with the earlier fast steps instead.
      • Confusing intermediates and catalysts: an intermediate is made then used up; a catalyst is used then made again.
      • Thinking a mechanism can be proved. Experiments can only show whether a mechanism agrees with the measured rate law.
      • Forgetting that the steps must add up to the overall reaction.

      Checking a mechanism

      A proposed mechanism must (1) add up to the overall equation, and (2) predict the experimental rate law. If the slow step is the first step, the rate law is read directly from it. If the slow step comes after a fast equilibrium, substitute for the intermediates using that equilibrium. Molecularity (unimolecular, bimolecular, termolecular) is the number of particles in an elementary step; it is almost always 1 or 2.

      Check yourself: which step determines the rate law of a multi-step mechanism?

      AP Unit 6

      Heat, temperature & phase changes

      Heat is energy moving because of a temperature difference. Temperature is how fast the particles are jiggling. They are not the same thing, and a heating curve shows why.

      The idea

      Pour hot soup into a cold bowl: energy flows from hot to cold until the temperatures match. That energy flow is heat (q). Temperature measures the average kinetic energy of the particles. When you add heat to a solid, the particles jiggle harder and the temperature rises: q = mcΔT, where c is the specific heat capacity, the energy needed to raise 1 g by 1 °C.

      But watch the heating curve: while ice melts, you keep adding heat and the temperature stays put at 0 °C. The energy isn't making particles faster; it is pulling them apart from their neighbors (breaking attractions). That energy is the enthalpy of fusion; for boiling, the enthalpy of vaporization. A plateau means "energy going into potential energy, not kinetic".

      Assumption upgrade Before, we assumed that adding heat always raises the temperature. Now we know that during a phase change heat goes into overcoming attractions, so the temperature stays constant and we need q = mΔH instead of q = mcΔT.
      Heat some water
      Temperature—
      State—
      Heat added—
      Equation in use—

      Try this

      Predict first, then drag the heat slider.

      1. Sit on the first plateau. Does the temperature change while you add more heat?

        What you should see

        The temperature stays at 0 °C while the ice melts: the particles leave their lattice sites one by one. The energy raises potential energy, not kinetic energy.

      2. Compare the two plateaus. Why is the boiling plateau so much longer?

        What you should see

        Boiling needs about 7 times as much energy per gram as melting (2260 J/g vs 334 J/g): the particles must be separated completely, not just loosened.

      3. Double the mass. What changes on the graph?

        What you should see

        The shape is the same but every segment is twice as long (twice as much energy for the same temperature change). The plateau temperatures don't change.

      Worked example

      How much heat is needed to turn 25.0 g of ice at −10.0 °C into water at 20.0 °C? (cice = 2.09 J/g·°C, cwater = 4.184 J/g·°C, ΔHfus = 334 J/g)

      Try it yourself first, then reveal one step at a time.

      1. Split the path. Warm the ice to 0 °C, melt it at 0 °C, then warm the water to 20 °C. Three pieces; add them.
      2. Warm the ice. q₁ = mcΔT = (25.0)(2.09)(10.0) = 522.5 J.
      3. Melt it. No temperature change, so use q₂ = mΔHfus = (25.0)(334) = 8350 J.
      4. Warm the water. q₃ = (25.0)(4.184)(20.0) = 2092 J. Total = 522.5 + 8350 + 2092 = 10 964.5 J ≈ 1.10×10⁴ J (11.0 kJ). The melting step is by far the biggest share.

      Common mistakes

      • Using q = mcΔT during a phase change. ΔT is zero there, but the heat isn't.
      • Forgetting a step: crossing several phases means several separate calculations, added up.
      • Mixing the specific heat of water with that of ice or steam. Each phase has its own c.
      • Using °C and K inconsistently. A change of 1 °C equals a change of 1 K, so ΔT is the same in both.
      • Saying "heat" and "temperature" mean the same. Heat is energy transferred; temperature is average kinetic energy.

      Why the plateau? A particle view

      Temperature tracks average kinetic energy. During melting the added energy loosens the lattice: the particles' potential energy rises while their kinetic energy (temperature) does not. Once every particle is free, further heat makes them move faster again. The attractions between particles are why ΔHvap is large for water: hydrogen bonds must be fully broken.

      Thermal equilibrium

      When two objects at different temperatures touch, heat flows from the hotter to the colder one until they reach the same temperature: thermal equilibrium. At the particle level, fast particles collide with slow ones and share kinetic energy until the average is equal. The total energy is conserved: the heat lost by one object equals the heat gained by the other. This is the idea behind every calorimetry problem in the next module.

      Check yourself: ice at 0 °C is melting while heat is added. What happens to the temperature?

      AP Unit 6

      Calorimetry

      You can't see energy, but you can see a thermometer. Calorimetry measures heat by watching how much a known amount of water warms up or cools down.

      The idea

      Energy is never lost: whatever one object gives up, another gains. Drop a hot metal into cool water. The metal cools, the water warms, and they settle at one temperature. The heat the metal loses equals the heat the water gains: qlost + qgained = 0. Since q = mcΔT for each, you can solve for the final temperature, or for an unknown specific heat.

      A reaction works the same way. If it releases heat, the solution around it warms up (exothermic, ΔH negative); if it absorbs heat, the solution gets cold (endothermic, ΔH positive). The water gained what the reaction lost, so qrxn = −qsolution. That is how a hot pack and a cold pack differ.

      Assumption upgrade Before, we assumed all the heat stays between the two objects. A real cup absorbs and leaks some. We ignore the cup for now, but a bomb calorimeter's heat capacity C (kJ/°C) is exactly how we account for it.
      Hot metal into water
      Final temperature—
      Heat lost by metal—
      Heat gained by water—
      Specific heat of metal—
      Dissolve a salt
      Temperature change—
      Heat absorbed by solution—
      ΔH of dissolving—
      Type (cold or hot pack)—

      Try this

      Predict the final temperature, then drop the metal in.

      1. Lead versus aluminum at the same mass and temperature. Which warms the water more?

        What you should see

        Aluminum, because it has a much larger specific heat (0.897 vs 0.129 J/g·°C): each gram holds about seven times as much heat. Lead's temperature drops a lot but it carries little energy.

      2. Use a lot more water. What happens to the final temperature?

        What you should see

        The final temperature ends closer to the water's starting temperature: a large mass of water changes temperature only a little for the same heat.

      3. Dissolve ammonium nitrate. Is it a hot pack or a cold pack?

        What you should see

        Cold. Dissolving NH₄NO₃ absorbs heat from the water (endothermic, ΔH positive). Instant cold packs use this.

      Worked example

      A 50.0 g piece of metal at 99.0 °C is dropped into 100.0 g of water at 21.0 °C. The final temperature is 24.0 °C. What is the specific heat of the metal? (cwater = 4.184 J/g·°C)

      Try it yourself first, then reveal one step at a time.

      1. Heat gained by the water. q = mcΔT = (100.0)(4.184)(24.0 − 21.0) = 1255 J.
      2. The metal lost the same amount. qmetal = −1255 J (negative because it lost heat).
      3. Solve for c. −1255 = (50.0)(c)(24.0 − 99.0) = (50.0)(c)(−75.0), so c = 1255 / 3750 = 0.335 J/g·°C.
      4. Check. The metal's ΔT is large and the water's is small, so the metal's c should be much less than water's. 0.335 ≪ 4.184 ✓.

      Common mistakes

      • Getting the sign wrong: the water's q is positive when it warms, the metal's q is negative; they add to zero.
      • Using ΔT = Tinitial − Tfinal. Always final minus initial.
      • Using the mass of the metal with the specific heat of water (or the reverse).
      • Forgetting that qrxn = −qsolution, and that ΔH is per mole, so divide by moles.
      • Forgetting that the solution's mass includes the dissolved solid.

      Coffee-cup and bomb calorimeters

      A coffee-cup calorimeter is open to the air, so it measures heat at constant pressure: q = ΔH. A bomb calorimeter is a sealed steel container in a water bath, so it measures heat at constant volume, and it comes with a calibrated heat capacity C (in kJ/°C): q = CΔT. In both cases the heat absorbed by the surroundings has the opposite sign of the heat released by the reaction.

      Check yourself: the temperature of a solution falls when a salt dissolves. What can you conclude?

      AP Unit 6

      Enthalpy, Hess's law & bond energies

      Chemical bonds are energy stores. Breaking them costs energy, making them gives energy back, and the difference is the heat of the reaction.

      The idea

      Think of a reaction as taking apart a Lego build and making a new one. Pulling apart the old bonds takes work (energy in); snapping together new bonds gives energy back (energy out). If more energy comes out than went in, the reaction is exothermic and ΔH is negative. If more went in than came out, it's endothermic and ΔH is positive.

      Enthalpy (H) is a state function: ΔH depends only on where you start and finish, not the route. That gives Hess's law: if a reaction can be written as the sum of other reactions, its ΔH is the sum of theirs. You can flip a reaction (flip the sign) or multiply it (multiply ΔH), just like the coefficients. You can find the ΔH of a reaction you can't measure by adding ones you can.

      Assumption upgrade Before, we measured heat directly with a calorimeter. Now we can calculate ΔH without doing the experiment, using Hess's law, standard enthalpies of formation, or average bond energies. Bond energies are averages over many molecules, so they give only an estimate.
      Formation enthalpiesΔH° = ΣnΔH°f(products) − ΣnΔH°f(reactants)ΔH°f of an element in its standard state = 0
      Bond energiesΔH ≈ Σ(bonds broken) − Σ(bonds formed)energy in minus energy out
      Build the reaction (Hess's law)
      Net equation—
      Sum of ΔH—
      Matches the target?—
      Break and make bonds
      Energy in (break)—
      Energy out (form)—
      ΔH—
      Enthalpy of formation

      Try this

      Predict first, then use the labs above.

      1. Do the first Hess puzzle. Which step did you have to flip? What happened to its sign?

        What you should see

        The step with CO as a reactant must run backward, so it is flipped (×−1) and its ΔH changes sign: −283.0 becomes +283.0.

      2. Watch the H₂ + Cl₂ reaction in the bond lab. Is the energy to break the bonds bigger or smaller than the energy released by forming them?

        What you should see

        Smaller: 679 kJ in (436 + 243) and 862 kJ out (2 × 431). The difference, −183 kJ, is released as heat, so the reaction is exothermic.

      3. Step through the combustion of methane with enthalpies of formation.

        What you should see

        Products minus reactants: [−393.5 + 2(−285.8)] − [−74.8 + 0] = −890.3 kJ. O₂ is an element, so its ΔH°f is zero.

      Worked example

      Find ΔH for C(s) + ½O₂(g) → CO(g) using: (1) C(s) + O₂(g) → CO₂(g), ΔH = −393.5 kJ; (2) CO(g) + ½O₂(g) → CO₂(g), ΔH = −283.0 kJ.

      Try it yourself first, then reveal one step at a time.

      1. Place each species. The target has C as a reactant, so keep equation (1) as written (C is on the left). The target has CO as a product, but in (2) CO is a reactant, so reverse (2).
      2. Reverse (2). CO₂ → CO + ½O₂, and flip the sign: ΔH = +283.0 kJ.
      3. Add. C + O₂ + CO₂ → CO₂ + CO + ½O₂. Cancel CO₂ on both sides and ½O₂ from the O₂: C + ½O₂ → CO. ✓
      4. Add the ΔH values. (−393.5) + (+283.0) = −110.5 kJ.

      Common mistakes

      • Forgetting to change the sign when reversing a reaction, or forgetting to multiply ΔH when multiplying the equation.
      • Subtracting in the wrong order: it's products minus reactants for formation enthalpies, but bonds broken minus bonds formed for bond energies.
      • Forgetting to multiply each ΔH°f by its coefficient.
      • Using ΔH°f ≠ 0 for an element in its standard state (O₂, H₂, C(graphite), Fe(s)...). Those are all zero.
      • Confusing the state: H₂O(l) and H₂O(g) have different ΔH°f.

      Per mole of what?

      ΔH in a balanced equation is for the reaction as written. If you write 2CH₄ + 4O₂ → …, ΔH doubles. To find the heat for a specific amount, convert it to moles, divide by the coefficient, and multiply by ΔH. Bond energies are always positive numbers (breaking costs energy), but the energy of formation is released, so subtract it.

      Check yourself: bonds broken cost 800 kJ and bonds formed release 950 kJ. What is ΔH?

      AP Unit 7

      Equilibrium & the equilibrium constant

      Many reactions run both ways. They don't finish: they settle into a balance. The equilibrium constant K says where that balance sits.

      The idea

      Picture a crowded dance floor with a door at each end. People walk in one door (reactants becoming products) as others walk out the other (products turning back). At first the traffic is lopsided. Over time the number of dancers inside stops changing, not because everyone stopped moving, but because the forward rate equals the reverse rate. That is dynamic equilibrium: motion continues, amounts don't change.

      The equilibrium constant, K, is the ratio of products to reactants at that balance, with each concentration raised to its coefficient: for aA + bB ⇌ cC + dD, K = [C]c[D]d / ([A]a[B]b). Big K (≫1) means products dominate; small K (≪1) means reactants dominate. At any moment, the same ratio computed with current concentrations is the reaction quotient Q. If Q < K the reaction runs forward; if Q > K it runs backward; if Q = K it is at equilibrium.

      Assumption upgrade Before, we assumed reactions go all the way to products (100% yield) and then stop. Now we know many stop part-way, with reactants and products coexisting, and the ratio is fixed by K at a given temperature.
      Watch a reaction settle
      [A]—
      [B]—
      Q—
      K—
      Status—
      Which way will it go?
      Q now—
      K—
      Prediction—

      Try this

      Predict first, then press Start.

      1. Start with only reactants and let it settle. Then restart with only products (same K). Do they reach the same mixture?

        What you should see

        Yes: the same ratio [B]/[A] = K. Equilibrium doesn't care which side you started from.

      2. Make K large (slide right). How much A is left at equilibrium?

        What you should see

        Almost none: with K = 10, about 9 of every 10 particles are B. A large K favors products, but at equilibrium the reaction is never 100% complete.

      3. Choose 2A ⇌ B. Why is K = [B]/[A]² and not [B]/[A]?

        What you should see

        Two A particles must come together to make each B, so [A] appears twice in the ratio (raised to its coefficient). The graph's forward-rate curve uses [A]².

      Worked example

      For N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) ⇌ 2NH₃(g), the equilibrium concentrations are [N₂] = 0.50 M, [H₂] = 0.20 M and [NH₃] = 0.15 M. Calculate Kc, then decide which way the reaction goes if [NH₃] is suddenly 0.60 M.

      Try it yourself first, then reveal one step at a time.

      1. Write the expression from the balanced equation: Kc = [NH₃]² / ([N₂][H₂]³).
      2. Plug in. Kc = (0.15)² / ((0.50)(0.20)³) = 0.0225 / (0.50 × 0.0080) = 0.0225 / 0.0040 = 5.6.
      3. Compute Q for the new mixture. Q = (0.60)² / ((0.50)(0.20)³) = 0.36 / 0.0040 = 90.
      4. Compare. Q (90) > K (5.6), so there is too much product. The reaction runs in reverse (toward reactants) until Q falls back to 5.6.

      Common mistakes

      • Thinking equilibrium means equal concentrations. It means constant concentrations, with equal rates.
      • Thinking the reaction stops. Both directions keep going at the same rate.
      • Including pure solids and pure liquids in K. Their concentrations are constant and are left out (including water as a solvent).
      • Forgetting to raise concentrations to their coefficients, or putting reactants on top.
      • Believing a large K means a fast reaction. K says where the balance is, not how quickly it gets there.
      • Assuming K changes when you add reactant. Only temperature changes K.

      Manipulating K

      Reverse the reaction: K becomes 1/K. Multiply the coefficients by n: K becomes Kn. Add two reactions: multiply their K values. For gases you can also write Kp with partial pressures, and Kp = Kc(RT)Δn, where Δn = moles of gas in products − moles of gas in reactants.

      Check yourself: what is true at dynamic equilibrium?

      AP Unit 7

      ICE tables & calculating equilibrium amounts

      Given K and a starting mixture, how much of each substance is there at equilibrium? An ICE table keeps the bookkeeping straight.

      The idea

      Think of a tug-of-war that begins with a lopsided rope. Initial: where the rope starts. Change: how far the reaction pulls to get to balance, expressed with one unknown, x, times each coefficient. Equilibrium: initial plus change. Plug the E row into K and solve for x.

      Below, you play the solver: slide x until Q reaches K. Q rises as the reaction moves forward, so there is exactly one x where Q = K. The graph shows this crossing. When K is small, x turns out small compared with the starting amount, and we may use the shortcut of dropping x from the subtraction, but only after checking the 5% rule.

      Assumption upgrade Before, we assumed "x is small" without testing it. Now we check: if x is more than 5% of the starting concentration, the shortcut fails and we must solve the full equation (often a quadratic).
      Slide x until Q = K
      Q at your x—
      K—
      Verdict—
      x ÷ start (5% rule)—

      Try this

      Predict x before you slide it.

      1. Make K very small and press Solve. How big is x compared with the starting amount?

        What you should see

        x is tiny (well under 5%), so ignoring x in the "start − x" term barely changes the answer: the shortcut and the exact answer agree.

      2. Now use K near 1 and see if the shortcut still works.

        What you should see

        x is a big fraction of the start, and the shortcut estimate is noticeably off. The 5% rule flags it: solve the full quadratic.

      3. Double the starting concentration with the same K. Does the percent that reacts stay the same?

        What you should see

        For N₂O₄ ⇌ 2NO₂ no: when one reactant makes two products, higher starting concentration means a smaller fraction reacts (Le Châtelier: more crowded favors fewer particles).

      Worked example

      N₂O₄(g) ⇌ 2NO₂(g), Kc = 0.36 at 100 °C. Starting from 0.100 M N₂O₄ with no NO₂, find the equilibrium concentrations.

      Try it yourself first, then reveal one step at a time.

      1. Set up the table. I: [N₂O₄] = 0.100, [NO₂] = 0. C: −x and +2x. E: 0.100 − x and 2x.
      2. Write K. 0.36 = (2x)² / (0.100 − x) = 4x² / (0.100 − x).
      3. Try the shortcut and check it. Drop x in the denominator: 4x² = 0.036, x ≈ 0.095, which is 95% of 0.100. Far above 5%, so the shortcut fails. Solve the quadratic.
      4. Quadratic. 4x² + 0.36x − 0.036 = 0. x = [−0.36 + √(0.36² + 4·4·0.036)] / 8 = [−0.36 + √0.7056] / 8 = (−0.36 + 0.84) / 8 = 0.060. So [NO₂] = 2x = 0.120 M and [N₂O₄] = 0.100 − 0.060 = 0.040 M.

      Common mistakes

      • Forgetting to multiply x by the coefficient (the table's change row is +2x, not +x).
      • Using the shortcut without checking: always test x ÷ start against 5%.
      • Reporting x as the answer. x is the change; the question usually wants the equilibrium concentrations (E row).
      • Putting the starting amounts of products into the table as zero when they aren't, or adding x to the wrong side.
      • Keeping a root that makes a concentration negative. Only one root is physically possible.

      The 5% rule in one line

      If K is small and the start is not tiny, then x ≪ start and you may write (start − x) ≈ start. Rule of thumb: the shortcut is acceptable when x/start < 5%. As a quick guide, that usually needs start/K to be about 400 or more.

      Check yourself: starting at 0.20 M, the shortcut gives x = 0.012 M. Is the shortcut acceptable?

      AP Unit 7

      Le Châtelier's principle

      Disturb a system at equilibrium and it fights back, shifting to partly undo the disturbance. Q and K tell you exactly why.

      The idea

      Imagine a seesaw perfectly balanced. Add a kid to one end and it tips; the other kids shuffle until the balance returns. A system at equilibrium does the same: add a substance and it shifts away from it; remove one and it shifts toward replacing it. Squeeze a gas mixture (smaller volume, higher pressure) and it shifts toward the side with fewer gas particles. Heat an endothermic reaction (treat heat as a reactant) and it shifts toward products; heat an exothermic reaction (heat is a product) and it shifts toward reactants.

      Underneath it all is a simple rule: a stress changes Q (or, for temperature, changes K). If Q ≠ K the reaction shifts until Q = K again. Changing concentrations or volume changes Q but not K. Only temperature changes K. A catalyst changes neither: it only gets you to equilibrium sooner.

      Assumption upgrade Before, we described equilibrium as fixed once reached. Now we see it is a balance that can be disturbed, and the shift follows from comparing Q with K, not from memorized rules alone.
      Disturb the equilibrium
      K now—
      Q now—
      Status—
      Predicted shift—

      Try this

      Predict the shift first. The graph and the Q-vs-K bar will show you.

      1. N₂O₄ ⇌ 2NO₂ is endothermic. Heat it. Which way does it shift, and what happens to K?

        What you should see

        Toward products (more brown NO₂). K increases: temperature is the one stress that changes K itself.

      2. Squeeze the same gas mixture (reduce the volume). Which way does it go?

        What you should see

        Toward N₂O₄, the side with fewer gas particles (1 vs 2). Concentrations jump at first because the volume dropped, then the shift partly relieves the pressure. K doesn't change.

      3. Haber process: remove ammonia as it forms.

        What you should see

        Q drops below K, so the reaction shifts right to make more NH₃. Industry removes NH₃ continuously for this reason.

      Worked example

      N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) ⇌ 2NH₃(g), ΔH = −92 kJ. For each stress, predict the shift: (a) add N₂, (b) raise the temperature, (c) decrease the volume.

      Try it yourself first, then reveal one step at a time.

      1. Add N₂ (a reactant). Q = [NH₃]²/([N₂][H₂]³) falls below K. The reaction shifts right (toward NH₃), using up some of the added N₂.
      2. Raise T. The reaction is exothermic, so heat is like a product. Adding heat is like adding product: shift left. Here K itself decreases.
      3. Decrease the volume. Gas concentrations increase. Reactants: 4 mol of gas; products: 2 mol. The system shifts toward the side with fewer moles: right. K is unchanged.
      4. Summary. (a) right, (b) left (and K gets smaller), (c) right. Only (b) changed the value of K.

      Common mistakes

      • Saying a concentration change or a volume change changes K. Only temperature does.
      • Thinking a catalyst shifts the equilibrium. It speeds up both directions equally and only helps reach equilibrium sooner.
      • Applying the "fewer moles" rule when the number of gas moles is equal on both sides (no shift), or when the pressure is raised by adding an inert gas at constant volume (no shift: the concentrations don't change).
      • Forgetting that pure solids and liquids don't count in the mole comparison.
      • Thinking the shift fully cancels the stress. It only partly offsets it.

      Temperature and K

      Raising T favors the endothermic direction, so K increases for an endothermic reaction (ΔH > 0) and decreases for an exothermic one. The van't Hoff relation makes this quantitative: ln(K₂/K₁) = −(ΔH/R)(1/T₂ − 1/T₁).

      Check yourself: an inert gas is added to an equilibrium mixture in a rigid container. What happens?

      AP Unit 7

      Solubility equilibria & Ksp

      "Insoluble" salts still dissolve a tiny bit. Ksp measures how much, and tells you when a precipitate will appear.

      The idea

      Drop a crystal of silver chloride in water. A few Ag⁺ and Cl⁻ ions break away; others stick back onto the crystal. Soon the rates match: a saturated solution, which is just an equilibrium, AgCl(s) ⇌ Ag⁺(aq) + Cl⁻(aq). Since the solid's concentration is constant, we leave it out: Ksp = [Ag⁺][Cl⁻]. The smaller the Ksp, the less dissolves.

      For a salt MaXb, Ksp = [M]a[X]b. The molar solubility s is how many moles dissolve per liter: [M] = a·s and [X] = b·s. If you already have one of the ions in the solution (a common ion), Le Châtelier pushes the equilibrium left and the salt dissolves less. And if you mix solutions so that Q > Ksp, a precipitate forms until Q falls back to Ksp.

      Assumption upgrade Before, "soluble" or "insoluble" from the solubility rules was a yes or no. Now we put numbers on it: insoluble salts have a small but nonzero solubility, and we can predict exactly when a precipitate forms.
      Dissolve a salt until saturated
      Ksp—
      Molar solubility s—
      [cation]—
      [anion]—
      Mass dissolving—

      The number of ions drawn is scaled so you can see the trend; real solutions at this level have far fewer ions than particles drawn.

      Mix two solutions: will it precipitate?
      [cation] after mixing—
      [anion] after mixing—
      Q—
      Ksp—
      Result—

      Try this

      Predict first, then use the labs.

      1. Add 0.10 M of the common chloride ion to AgCl. How does the solubility change?

        What you should see

        It drops by about four orders of magnitude, from 1.3×10⁻⁵ M to 1.8×10⁻⁹ M. Extra Cl⁻ pushes AgCl(s) ⇌ Ag⁺ + Cl⁻ to the left, so less dissolves.

      2. Compare Ag₂CrO₄ (Ksp 1.1×10⁻¹²) with AgCl (1.8×10⁻¹⁰). Which has the lower solubility?

        What you should see

        Surprise: Ag₂CrO₄ is more soluble (6.5×10⁻⁵ M vs 1.3×10⁻⁵ M) despite its smaller Ksp, because it has a different formula type. You can compare Ksp values directly only for salts with the same number of ions.

      3. Mix 0.001 M Ag⁺ and 0.001 M Cl⁻ in equal volumes. Precipitate?

        What you should see

        After mixing, each ion is 5×10⁻⁴ M, so Q = 2.5×10⁻⁷, which is much larger than Ksp (1.8×10⁻¹⁰): a precipitate forms.

      Worked example

      Ksp of PbI₂ is 9.8×10⁻⁹. (a) Find its molar solubility in pure water. (b) Find its solubility in 0.050 M KI.

      Try it yourself first, then reveal one step at a time.

      1. Equilibrium and expression. PbI₂(s) ⇌ Pb²⁺ + 2I⁻, Ksp = [Pb²⁺][I⁻]².
      2. (a) Use s. [Pb²⁺] = s, [I⁻] = 2s. Ksp = s(2s)² = 4s³ = 9.8×10⁻⁹, so s = (2.45×10⁻⁹)1/3 = 1.35×10⁻³ M.
      3. (b) Add the common ion. [I⁻] = 0.050 + 2s ≈ 0.050 (s is tiny). Ksp = s(0.050)² so s = 9.8×10⁻⁹ / 2.5×10⁻³ = 3.9×10⁻⁶ M.
      4. Check. 2s = 7.8×10⁻⁶ ≪ 0.050 ✓ (far under 5%). The common ion cut the solubility by a factor of about 350.

      Common mistakes

      • Forgetting that [X] = b·s: for PbI₂ the iodide concentration is 2s, and it is squared in Ksp.
      • Comparing Ksp values to rank solubilities when the salts have different formulas (like AgCl and Ag₂CrO₄).
      • Forgetting dilution when two solutions are mixed: concentrations drop before you compute Q.
      • Including the solid in the Ksp expression.
      • Calling Q > Ksp "saturated". Q = Ksp is saturated; Q > Ksp is supersaturated and a precipitate forms.

      Other ways to change solubility

      Adding acid dissolves salts whose anion is a base (CaCO₃, Mg(OH)₂, many fluorides and sulfides): H⁺ removes the anion, pulling the equilibrium right. Complex-ion formation (like Ag⁺ with NH₃) works the same way. Temperature changes Ksp itself, as with any K.

      Check yourself: AgCl is dissolved in 0.10 M NaCl instead of pure water. Its solubility is…

      AP Unit 8

      Acids, bases, pH & strong acids

      Acid-base chemistry is proton hopping. Water itself takes part, and pH is just a convenient way to count the hydronium ions.

      The idea

      A Brønsted–Lowry acid is a proton (H⁺) donor; a base is a proton acceptor. Every acid-base reaction is a proton hand-off, and each side has a conjugate partner: the acid becomes its conjugate base, the base becomes its conjugate acid. In water, a free H⁺ doesn't exist alone: it sticks to a water molecule, making hydronium, H₃O⁺.

      Even pure water does this a tiny bit: two H₂O molecules swap a proton (autoionization), giving Kw = [H₃O⁺][OH⁻] = 1.0×10⁻¹⁴ at 25 °C. pH = −log[H₃O⁺], and pOH = −log[OH⁻], with pH + pOH = 14 at 25 °C. A strong acid (HCl, HBr, HI, HNO₃, HClO₄, H₂SO₄ for its first proton) gives up its proton completely, so [H₃O⁺] equals the acid's concentration. Strong bases (hydroxides of group 1, and Ca, Sr, Ba) dissociate completely too.

      Assumption upgrade Before, pH = −log(c) for a strong acid. Now we notice water supplies 10⁻⁷ M of H₃O⁺ too. At normal concentrations that doesn't matter, but for a very dilute acid (10⁻⁸ M) it does: the pH of 10⁻⁸ M HCl is about 6.98, not 8, because an acid can't make the solution basic.
      Proton hand-off
      Acid (gives H⁺)—
      Base (takes H⁺)—
      Conjugate base—
      Conjugate acid—
      The pH of a strong acid or base
      [H₃O⁺]—
      [OH⁻]—
      pH—
      pOH—
      Simple formula gives—

      Try this

      Predict, then slide the controls.

      1. Dilute a strong acid by a factor of 10. How much does the pH change?

        What you should see

        Going from 10⁻² M to 10⁻³ M raises the pH by exactly 1 (from 2 to 3): each factor of 10 in concentration is one pH unit. Check by sliding.

      2. Dilute HCl all the way to 10⁻⁸ M. Does the pH go above 7?

        What you should see

        No: about 6.98. Water contributes 10⁻⁷ M of H₃O⁺ and the acid adds to that; an acid can never make the pH basic.

      3. Hot water: set the temperature to 50 °C and look at a neutral solution.

        What you should see

        Neutral pH is about 6.63 at 50 °C, not 7, because Kw grows with temperature. Neutral means [H₃O⁺] = [OH⁻], not "pH = 7".

      Worked example

      What is the pH of 0.025 M Ba(OH)₂ at 25 °C?

      Try it yourself first, then reveal one step at a time.

      1. Strong base: dissociates completely. Ba(OH)₂ → Ba²⁺ + 2OH⁻.
      2. Count hydroxide. Each formula unit gives 2 OH⁻, so [OH⁻] = 2 × 0.025 = 0.050 M.
      3. pOH. pOH = −log(0.050) = 1.30.
      4. pH. pH = 14.00 − 1.30 = 12.70.

      Common mistakes

      • Forgetting to count the number of OH⁻ per formula unit (Ba(OH)₂ and Ca(OH)₂ give 2).
      • Giving a pH above 7 for a very dilute acid (or below 7 for a very dilute base).
      • Using pH + pOH = 14 at temperatures other than 25 °C: it equals −log Kw.
      • Saying H⁺ "floats free" in water. It's H₃O⁺, but H⁺ and H₃O⁺ are interchangeable on the AP exam.
      • Mixing up acid and conjugate: an acid's conjugate is a base (it has one fewer H⁺).

      Strong acids and bases to know

      Strong acids: HCl, HBr, HI, HNO₃, HClO₄, and H₂SO₄ (first proton only). Strong bases: LiOH, NaOH, KOH, RbOH, CsOH, Ca(OH)₂, Sr(OH)₂, Ba(OH)₂. For a strong acid, [H₃O⁺] = c; for a strong base, [OH⁻] = (number of OH) × c. Everything else is weak. A conjugate pair differs by exactly one H⁺: strong acids have negligible conjugate bases; weak acids have weak conjugate bases.

      Check yourself: what is the pH of 1.0×10⁻³ M HNO₃?

      AP Unit 8

      Weak acids & bases, Ka and Kb

      Most acids don't give up all their protons. A weak acid is a small chemical tug-of-war, and Ka says who is winning.

      The idea

      A strong acid is like a person who throws every ball they're holding. A weak acid holds on tight: only a few molecules per thousand hand over their proton. Acetic acid in vinegar is the classic example: in 0.10 M vinegar only about 1.3% of the molecules ionize, so almost all the acid is still sitting there as CH₃COOH.

      The equilibrium HA + H₂O ⇌ H₃O⁺ + A⁻ has Ka = [H₃O⁺][A⁻]/[HA]. A bigger Ka means a stronger acid. Weak bases work the same way with Kb: B + H₂O ⇌ BH⁺ + OH⁻. An acid and its conjugate base are linked by Ka × Kb = Kw: the stronger the acid, the weaker its conjugate base. Interestingly, the fraction that ionizes goes up when you dilute: more room for the ions to spread out.

      Assumption upgrade Before, we assumed acids were strong, so [H₃O⁺] equalled the acid concentration. Now an acid can be weak, and [H₃O⁺] must come from an equilibrium (Ka) and an ICE table, with the "x is small" check.
      How many molecules actually ionize?
      pH—
      % ionized—
      Ka or Kb—
      K of the conjugate (Kb or Ka)—
      1 in every…—

      Try this

      Predict first, then compare the two beakers.

      1. Look at 0.10 M acetic acid. How many molecules ionize?

        What you should see

        About 1 in 75 (1.3%). The pH is about 2.88, far higher than the pH 1.00 of 0.10 M HCl, because most acetic acid stays whole.

      2. Dilute acetic acid tenfold, then tenfold again. What happens to the percent ionized?

        What you should see

        It rises (about 4% at 0.001 M): dilution favors the side with more particles, so a larger fraction of the molecules ionize. (The pH rises less than a strong acid's would.)

      3. Compare HF with HCN at the same concentration.

        What you should see

        HCN (Ka = 4.9×10⁻¹⁰) barely ionizes at all: about 1 molecule in 45 000. Its pH is near 5.2, just above that of water plus a trace of acid.

      Worked example

      Find the pH and percent ionization of 0.10 M acetic acid. Ka = 1.8×10⁻⁵.

      Try it yourself first, then reveal one step at a time.

      1. ICE. CH₃COOH ⇌ H⁺ + CH₃COO⁻. I: 0.10, 0, 0. C: −x, +x, +x. E: 0.10 − x, x, x.
      2. Write Ka. 1.8×10⁻⁵ = x² / (0.10 − x).
      3. Try the shortcut. 0.10 − x ≈ 0.10, so x² = 1.8×10⁻⁶ and x = 1.34×10⁻³ M. Check: 1.34×10⁻³ / 0.10 = 1.3%, which is under 5%. ✓
      4. Answer. pH = −log(1.34×10⁻³) = 2.87 and percent ionization = 1.3%. (A quadratic gives 2.88; the shortcut is fine.)

      Common mistakes

      • Using [H₃O⁺] = c for a weak acid. That is only for strong acids.
      • Skipping the 5% check, especially for fairly strong weak acids (HF, HNO₂) at low concentration.
      • Reporting x as the pH instead of −log x.
      • Mixing up Ka and Kb: a weak base gives OH⁻, so x is [OH⁻] and you get pOH first.
      • Calling a weak acid "dilute" and a strong acid "concentrated". Strength (how much ionizes) is not the same as concentration (how much is there).

      Why are some acids stronger than others?

      Down a group (HF < HCl < HBr < HI) bond strength dominates: the longer, weaker H–X bond lets go of its proton more easily. Across a period (CH₄ < NH₃ < H₂O < HF) electronegativity dominates. For oxyacids (HClO < HClO₂ < HClO₃ < HClO₄), more oxygen atoms (or more electronegative substituents) pull electron density away from the O–H bond and stabilize the conjugate base. In carboxylic acids, a chlorine on the carbon increases acidity.

      Check yourself: HF has Ka = 6.8×10⁻⁴. What is Kb of F⁻?

      AP Unit 8

      Salt solutions, polyprotic acids & species vs pH

      "Neutral salt" doesn't mean a neutral solution. The ions of a salt can be acids or bases themselves, and the pH decides which form of an acid is actually in the beaker.

      The idea

      When a salt dissolves, you get its cation and its anion. Ask where each came from. An ion from a strong acid or base (Na⁺, K⁺, Cl⁻, NO₃⁻, Br⁻, ClO₄⁻) is a bystander: it does nothing to the pH. An ion from a weak acid or base is not. The conjugate base of a weak acid (CH₃COO⁻, F⁻, CO₃²⁻) takes protons from water and makes OH⁻, so the solution is basic. The conjugate acid of a weak base (NH₄⁺) gives protons to water and makes H₃O⁺, so it is acidic. Small, highly charged metal ions such as Al³⁺ and Fe³⁺ pull on the O–H bonds of their hydrating water and are acidic as well.

      The strength of that effect comes from Ka × Kb = Kw. The weaker the parent acid, the stronger its conjugate base. And for an acid with more than one removable proton (a polyprotic acid such as H₃PO₄ or H₂CO₃) each proton comes off with its own Ka, always Ka1 > Ka2 > Ka3, because it is harder to remove a proton from an ion that is already negative. Which form dominates depends on the pH compared with each pKa: below the pKa the protonated form wins; above it, the deprotonated form wins; at pH = pKa they are equal.

      Assumption upgrade Before, we assumed a salt solution is neutral (we only used it to make precipitates and spectators). Now we know the ions themselves can be weak acids or bases, so a salt like sodium acetate has a pH above 7 and ammonium chloride below 7.
      Acidic, basic or neutral salt?
      Cation from—
      Anion from—
      Solution is—
      pH—
      Which form is in the flask?

      Try this

      Predict, then check.

      1. Dissolve sodium acetate. Is the solution acidic or basic? Why?

        What you should see

        Basic (pH about 8.9 at 0.10 M). Na⁺ is a bystander, but CH₃COO⁻ is the conjugate base of a weak acid and pulls a proton off water: CH₃COO⁻ + H₂O ⇌ CH₃COOH + OH⁻.

      2. Dissolve ammonium chloride.

        What you should see

        Acidic (pH about 5.1). Cl⁻ is a bystander; NH₄⁺ is the conjugate acid of weak NH₃ and gives a proton to water: NH₄⁺ + H₂O ⇌ NH₃ + H₃O⁺.

      3. Phosphoric acid at pH 7: which form dominates?

        What you should see

        H₂PO₄⁻ and HPO₄²⁻ are about equal at pH 7.2 (the second pKa). Around neutral pH the two middle forms dominate, which is why phosphate buffers work in cells.

      Worked example

      Find the pH of 0.10 M sodium acetate. (Ka of acetic acid = 1.8×10⁻⁵)

      Try it yourself first, then reveal one step at a time.

      1. Which ion reacts? Na⁺ comes from a strong base (a bystander). CH₃COO⁻ is the conjugate base of a weak acid, so it reacts with water: CH₃COO⁻ + H₂O ⇌ CH₃COOH + OH⁻.
      2. Find Kb. Kb = Kw/Ka = 1.0×10⁻¹⁴ / 1.8×10⁻⁵ = 5.6×10⁻¹⁰.
      3. ICE table. Kb = x²/(0.10 − x) ≈ x²/0.10, so x = [OH⁻] = √(5.6×10⁻¹⁰ × 0.10) = 7.5×10⁻⁶ M (far under 5% of 0.10).
      4. pH. pOH = −log(7.5×10⁻⁶) = 5.13, so pH = 14.00 − 5.13 = 8.87. Basic, as predicted.

      Common mistakes

      • Calling every salt solution neutral. Only a salt made from a strong acid and a strong base (NaCl, KNO₃) is neutral.
      • Using Ka of the parent acid directly for the anion. The anion is a base: use Kb = Kw/Ka.
      • Letting the cation of a strong base (Na⁺) or the anion of a strong acid (Cl⁻) hydrolyze. They don't.
