      • For a polyprotic acid, treating the second proton as if it matters for pH. Usually Ka1 ≫ Ka2, so the pH comes from the first dissociation alone.
      • Mixing up the direction: below the pKa (more acidic solution) the protonated form dominates.

      Cheat sheet

      Strong acid + strong base parent: neutral (NaCl). Strong base + weak acid: basic (NaCH₃COO, NaF, Na₂CO₃, NaCN). Weak base + strong acid: acidic (NH₄Cl). Weak acid + weak base: compare Ka of the cation with Kb of the anion; NH₄CH₃COO is nearly neutral because Ka(NH₄⁺) ≈ Kb(CH₃COO⁻). Small, highly charged cations (Al³⁺, Fe³⁺, Cu²⁺): acidic.

      Species vs pH: pH = pKa + log([A⁻]/[HA]), so [A⁻]/[HA] = 10(pH − pKa). Two pH units below the pKa the acid is 99% protonated; two units above, 99% deprotonated. This is also how indicators work: the two forms HIn and In⁻ have different colors, and the color changes where pH ≈ pKa of the indicator.

      An amphiprotic species can act as an acid or a base: water, HCO₃⁻, H₂PO₄⁻, HSO₄⁻ (as an acid only toward water in practice), HPO₄²⁻. A solution of such an ion is often close to the average of the two neighboring pKa values.

      Check yourself: a solution of NaF in water is…

      AP Unit 8

      Titration curves & indicators

      Add base drop by drop to an acid and watch the pH. The curve tells you the concentration, the strength of the acid, and which indicator to use.

      The idea

      In a titration you add a solution of known concentration (the titrant) from a burette until the reaction is exactly complete, the equivalence point: moles of base added equal moles of acid originally present. From the volume you can work out the unknown concentration. An indicator changes color near the pH of the equivalence point to signal the endpoint.

      The shape of the curve depends on the acid. Strong acid + strong base: the pH stays low, shoots up through 7 at the equivalence point, and levels off. Weak acid + strong base: the start is higher, a gentle buffer region follows (the pH barely moves because HA and A⁻ are both present), and the equivalence point is above 7 because A⁻ is a weak base. At half-equivalence exactly half the HA has become A⁻, so [HA] = [A⁻] and pH = pKa.

      Assumption upgrade Before, the equivalence point was always at pH 7 (strong acid and strong base). Now we know it depends on what is left in the flask: a weak acid's conjugate base makes the equivalence point basic, and a weak base's conjugate acid makes it acidic. We need an indicator that changes color near that pH.
      Titrate it
      pH—
      Where we are—
      Equivalence at—
      pH at equivalence—
      Half-equivalence pH—

      Try this

      Predict the curve, then drip.

      1. Titrate acetic acid and look at the half-equivalence point. What is the pH there?

        What you should see

        pH = 4.74 = pKa of acetic acid (Ka = 1.8×10⁻⁵). Half the acid has turned into acetate, so [HA] = [A⁻] and the ratio in Henderson–Hasselbalch is 1.

      2. Titrate HCl with NaOH, then pick the wrong indicator for acetic acid (methyl orange).

        What you should see

        The equivalence point of acetic acid is near pH 8.7, but methyl orange has already changed color around pH 3 to 4.4, long before. You'd stop far too early. Phenolphthalein (8.2–10) is the right choice.

      3. Titrate HCN (Ka = 4.9×10⁻¹⁰). Is there a sharp jump?

        What you should see

        Hardly any: a very weak acid gives only a small, rounded rise at equivalence, so no ordinary indicator marks it well. Titrations work best when Ka is not too small.

      Worked example

      25.00 mL of 0.100 M acetic acid (Ka = 1.8×10⁻⁵) is titrated with 0.100 M NaOH. Find (a) the volume at equivalence, (b) the pH after adding 10.00 mL, and (c) the pH at equivalence.

      Try it yourself first, then reveal one step at a time.

      1. (a) Equivalence. n(HA) = 0.02500 × 0.100 = 2.50 mmol. The base is 1:1, so V = 2.50 mmol / 0.100 M = 25.00 mL.
      2. (b) Before equivalence: a buffer. OH⁻ added = 10.00 × 0.100 = 1.00 mmol, which converts 1.00 mmol HA into A⁻: HA = 1.50 mmol, A⁻ = 1.00 mmol. pH = pKa + log(A⁻/HA) = 4.74 + log(1.00/1.50) = 4.74 − 0.18 = 4.56.
      3. (c) At equivalence: only A⁻. [A⁻] = 2.50 mmol / 50.0 mL = 0.0500 M. Kb = 1.0×10⁻¹⁴ / 1.8×10⁻⁵ = 5.6×10⁻¹⁰, so [OH⁻] = √(5.6×10⁻¹⁰ × 0.0500) = 5.3×10⁻⁶ M.
      4. Convert. pOH = 5.28, so pH = 14 − 5.28 = 8.72. Above 7, as expected for a weak acid; phenolphthalein is a good indicator.

      Common mistakes

      • Assuming the equivalence point is always pH 7. Only strong-acid/strong-base titrations are neutral there.
      • Using Henderson–Hasselbalch at the equivalence point or after it. It applies only in the buffer region, where both HA and A⁻ are present in comparable amounts.
      • Forgetting that the total volume increases as titrant is added when you compute concentrations.
      • Using volumes where moles are needed. Always compute moles (mmol works well), then divide by total volume.
      • Mixing up the equivalence point (moles equal) and the endpoint (indicator color change). A good indicator makes them very close.

      Four regions of a weak-acid curve

      (1) Start: only HA; pH from Ka. (2) Buffer region: HA and A⁻; use Henderson–Hasselbalch with moles. At half-equivalence pH = pKa. (3) Equivalence: only A⁻; pH from Kb of A⁻. (4) Past equivalence: excess OH⁻ controls the pH, and the weak base contributes almost nothing.

      Check yourself: at the half-equivalence point of a weak acid titration, pH equals…

      AP Unit 8

      Buffers

      Your blood stays near pH 7.4 even though you eat acidic food all day. A buffer is a chemical shock absorber.

      The idea

      A buffer holds both a weak acid (HA) and its conjugate base (A⁻) in comparable amounts. Add a strong acid and the A⁻ soaks it up (A⁻ + H₃O⁺ → HA). Add a strong base and the HA neutralizes it (HA + OH⁻ → A⁻ + H₂O). Either way the dangerous H₃O⁺ or OH⁻ is converted into the weak partner, so the pH barely moves. Think of two sponges, one for acid and one for base.

      The pH of a buffer comes from the Henderson–Hasselbalch equation: pH = pKa + log([A⁻]/[HA]). If the two are equal the pH equals the pKa. The ratio, not the absolute amounts, sets the pH; the absolute amounts set the capacity: how much strong acid or base the buffer can take before one component runs out. A buffer works best when the pH is within one unit of its pKa.

      Assumption upgrade Before, adding a strong acid always meant a big pH drop. Now we know a solution containing both HA and A⁻ converts the added acid or base into the weak partner, and the pH changes only through the small change in the ratio.
      Stress a buffer
      Buffer pH—
      Plain water pH—
      Buffer pH change—
      HA / A⁻ left (mmol)—

      Pick a buffer for a target pH

      Try this

      Predict first, then slide.

      1. Add a bit of strong acid to the buffer, then to plain water. Compare the pH change.

        What you should see

        The buffer pH moves by only a few hundredths, while plain water falls about 5 pH units (from 7 to roughly 2). The added H₃O⁺ is converted to HA.

      2. Make the buffer 10 times more dilute. What happens to its pH and to its resistance?

        What you should see

        The starting pH doesn't change (only the ratio matters), but the buffer's capacity shrinks tenfold, so the same amount of acid makes a much larger change. If it overloads, the pH plunges.

      3. Choose a ratio of 10:1 and then of 1:10. How far from the pKa is the pH?

        What you should see

        Exactly 1 pH unit above the pKa for 10:1 and 1 unit below for 1:10. Beyond that, the buffer is too one-sided to resist both acid and base well.

      Worked example

      A buffer contains 0.20 M acetic acid and 0.30 M acetate (pKa = 4.74), 1.00 L in total. (a) Find the pH. (b) Find the pH after adding 0.050 mol of HCl.

      Try it yourself first, then reveal one step at a time.

      1. (a) Henderson–Hasselbalch. pH = 4.74 + log(0.30 / 0.20) = 4.74 + 0.18 = 4.92.
      2. (b) Do the stoichiometry first. H₃O⁺ reacts completely with acetate: A⁻ + H₃O⁺ → HA. Moles: A⁻ = 0.30 − 0.050 = 0.25; HA = 0.20 + 0.050 = 0.25.
      3. Then equilibrium (H–H). pH = 4.74 + log(0.25 / 0.25) = 4.74.
      4. Compare. The pH fell by only 0.18, whereas 0.050 mol HCl in 1.00 L of plain water would give pH 1.30, a drop of nearly 6 units.

      Common mistakes

      • Skipping the stoichiometry step: when you add strong acid or base, first let it react completely, then use Henderson–Hasselbalch with the new moles.
      • Using a mixture of a strong acid and its conjugate base (HCl + NaCl) and calling it a buffer. The acid must be weak.
      • Mixing up which way the ratio goes: it is [conjugate base]/[acid]. More base means a higher pH.
      • Thinking dilution changes a buffer's pH. It changes capacity, not the ratio (to a good approximation).
      • Adding more strong acid than there is A⁻. Past that, the buffer is exhausted and the pH crashes.

      Making a buffer

      Three routes give the same result: mix the weak acid with a salt of its conjugate base; mix the weak base with a salt of its conjugate acid; or start with the weak acid and add less than enough strong base to neutralize it (that makes A⁻ in place). Choose a pair with a pKa within about one unit of the target pH, then set the ratio [A⁻]/[HA] = 10(pH − pKa).

      Check yourself: which mixture is a buffer?

      AP Unit 9

      Entropy & microstates

      Why does a gas fill its container, and why does a hot cup of coffee cool down? Not because anything pulls: there are just overwhelmingly more ways for it to happen.

      The idea

      Shuffle a deck of cards and you will never get them back in perfect order. It isn't forbidden; it is just wildly unlikely, because there is only one ordered arrangement and an astronomical number of messy ones. Entropy (S) measures how many ways (microstates, W) the energy and particles of a system can be arranged: S = kB ln W. More ways means higher entropy, and systems drift toward the arrangements that are most numerous.

      Entropy is larger for gases than liquids than solids (particles roam), for more moles of gas, for higher temperature (more ways to share energy), for larger or more complex molecules, and when substances mix or dissolve. The second law says the total entropy of the universe never decreases in a spontaneous process. A system can lose entropy (like water freezing) only if it dumps enough heat to the surroundings to raise their entropy by more.

      Assumption upgrade Before, we thought reactions run downhill in energy only (exothermic = spontaneous). Now we see energy isn't the whole story: some endothermic processes (ice melting, salts dissolving) are spontaneous because they increase entropy. Next, Gibbs free energy combines both.
      Count the ways
      In left half now—
      Ways to arrange that (W)—
      Total possible arrangements—
      S = kB ln W—
      Chance all return left—
      Entropy change of a reaction
      Predict first:

      Try this

      Predict first, then check.

      1. Open the partition with 4 particles, then with 40. Which one ever returns to "all on the left"?

        What you should see

        With 4 particles it happens now and then (1 in 16). With 40 it never will: the chance is (½)⁴⁰, about 1 in a trillion. With a mole of gas, it is impossible for all practical purposes. That is the second law.

      2. Look at the graph of arrangements. Which split has the most arrangements?

        What you should see

        The even split. There are far more ways to have about half on each side than all on one side, so the particles spend nearly all their time near the middle.

      3. Step through the reaction CaCO₃ → CaO + CO₂. Predict the sign of ΔS first.

        What you should see

        Positive: a solid makes a solid plus a free gas. One mole of gas appears from nothing, so ΔS° = +160.6 J/mol·K.

      Worked example

      Calculate ΔS° for N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) → 2NH₃(g) using S° (J/mol·K): N₂ 191.6, H₂ 130.6, NH₃ 192.5.

      Try it yourself first, then reveal one step at a time.

      1. Predict the sign. 4 mol of gas become 2 mol of gas, so there is less disorder: ΔS should be negative.
      2. Products. ΣnS°(products) = 2 × 192.5 = 385.0 J/K.
      3. Reactants. ΣnS°(reactants) = 191.6 + 3 × 130.6 = 191.6 + 391.8 = 583.4 J/K.
      4. Subtract. ΔS° = 385.0 − 583.4 = −198.4 J/K (per mole of reaction as written). Negative, as predicted. Note the units: J/K, not kJ.

      Common mistakes

      • Saying "entropy means messiness" and stopping there. Count the available arrangements of particles and energy.
      • Giving ΔS in kJ with ΔH in kJ: S is usually in J/K, ΔH in kJ. Convert before combining.
      • Forgetting the coefficient: ΔS° = ΣnS°(products) − ΣnS°(reactants).
      • Assuming the entropy of an element in its standard state is zero. (That is ΔH°f; elements have positive absolute S°. Only a perfect crystal at 0 K has S = 0.)
      • Thinking the entropy of a system can never decrease. It can, if the surroundings gain more than the system loses.

      Quick rules for the sign of ΔS

      Gas formed or more moles of gas: ΔS > 0. Fewer moles of gas: ΔS < 0. Melting, vaporizing, dissolving a solid: ΔS > 0 (usually). Freezing, condensing, precipitating: ΔS < 0. Heating a substance: ΔS > 0. The third law sets the zero: a perfect crystal at 0 K has S = 0, so every substance has a definite absolute entropy S° at 298 K.

      Check yourself: which has the greatest entropy at 1 mol each?

      AP Unit 9

      Gibbs free energy & spontaneity

      Two forces decide whether a process happens on its own: the drive to release energy and the drive to spread out. Gibbs free energy adds them up, and temperature decides who wins.

      The idea

      Ice melts above 0 °C and freezes below it. The energy side says "stay frozen" (melting costs heat) while the disorder side says "melt" (liquid has more entropy). At low temperature energy wins; at high temperature disorder wins; at 0 °C they tie. Temperature multiplies the entropy term, so heat helps entropy-driven processes.

      That tug-of-war is ΔG = ΔH − TΔS. A process is thermodynamically favorable (spontaneous) when ΔG < 0, at equilibrium when ΔG = 0, and unfavorable when ΔG > 0. The signs of ΔH and ΔS give four cases: (−, +) always favorable; (+, −) never; (−, −) favorable only at low T; (+, +) favorable only at high T. Where the sign flips is at T = ΔH/ΔS. Note "spontaneous" says nothing about speed: diamond turning into graphite is favorable but takes forever (the activation energy is huge).

      Assumption upgrade Before, exothermic meant "will happen". Now we need both ΔH and ΔS, and the temperature. ΔG° also connects to K: ΔG° = −RT ln K, so the thermodynamics of a reaction fixes where its equilibrium sits.
      GibbsΔG° = ΔH° − TΔS°ΔS° in J/K → convert to kJ/K
      EquilibriumΔG° = −RT ln KR = 8.314 J/mol·K
      Non-standardΔG = ΔG° + RT ln Qsign of ΔG sets the direction
      Energy vs disorder
      ΔG—
      Verdict—
      Crossover T = ΔH/ΔS—
      K (from ΔG)—
      ΔS of universe—
      Which way will it go? ΔG = ΔG° + RT ln Q
      ΔG° (at the T above)—
      K—
      ΔG at this Q—
      Direction—

      Try this

      Predict where it flips, then slide the temperature.

      1. Melt ice: at what temperature does ΔG change sign?

        What you should see

        At about 273 K (0 °C), where T = ΔH/ΔS = 6010/22.0. Below that ΔG is positive (ice is stable); above it, negative (melting is favorable).

      2. Make ammonia. Is it better to run the reaction hot or cold, thermodynamically?

        What you should see

        Cold: ΔH is negative and ΔS is negative, so the reaction is favorable only below about 464 K. (Industry runs it hot anyway to make it fast, and uses pressure to compensate.)

      3. Choose ozone formation, 3O₂ → 2O₃. Does any temperature work?

        What you should see

        No: ΔH is positive and ΔS is negative, so ΔG is positive at every temperature. It never happens spontaneously (UV light provides the energy instead).

      Worked example

      For CaCO₃(s) → CaO(s) + CO₂(g), ΔH° = +178.3 kJ and ΔS° = +160.6 J/K. (a) Is it favorable at 298 K? (b) At what temperature does it become favorable?

      Try it yourself first, then reveal one step at a time.

      1. Units first. ΔS° = 160.6 J/K = 0.1606 kJ/K, so it matches ΔH in kJ.
      2. (a) At 298 K. ΔG° = 178.3 − (298)(0.1606) = 178.3 − 47.9 = +130.4 kJ. Positive: not favorable at room temperature (limestone doesn't decompose on its own).
      3. (b) Find the flip. ΔG° = 0 when T = ΔH/ΔS = 178.3 / 0.1606 = 1110 K (about 837 °C).
      4. Interpret. Both ΔH and ΔS are positive, so the reaction is favorable above 1110 K, where the entropy term (the CO₂ gas) outweighs the energy cost. This is why lime kilns run hot.

      Common mistakes

      • Mixing units: ΔH in kJ and ΔS in J/K. Convert ΔS to kJ/K (divide by 1000) before multiplying by T.
      • Using °C instead of kelvin for T.
      • Equating "spontaneous" with "fast" or "happens quickly". It only means thermodynamically favorable.
      • Saying ΔG° > 0 means no reaction at all. It means the equilibrium lies toward reactants (K < 1); a little product still forms.
      • Confusing ΔG° with ΔG. ΔG° is for standard conditions (Q = 1); ΔG depends on Q and is zero at equilibrium.

      Thermodynamic vs kinetic

      ΔG tells you the direction a system will go and how far (through K). The activation energy tells you how fast. A reaction with large negative ΔG but a high barrier (diamond to graphite, H₂ + O₂ → H₂O at room temperature) can sit for ages until a spark or catalyst helps.

      Thermodynamic vs kinetic control, and coupled reactions

      ΔG tells you whether a reaction can go, not how fast. A reaction can be thermodynamically favorable (ΔG < 0) but kinetically slow because of a large activation energy: diamond → graphite, or H₂ + O₂ → H₂O at room temperature. When a reaction can give two products, the one that forms fastest (lower Ea) is the kinetic product; the one that is more stable (lower ΔG) is the thermodynamic product, which wins if the reaction is reversible and given enough time.

      An unfavorable reaction (ΔG > 0) can be driven by coupling it to a favorable one when the two share an intermediate. The overall ΔG is the sum: ΔGtotal = ΔG₁ + ΔG₂. If the sum is negative, the pair proceeds. Cells do this constantly, using ATP → ADP + Pᵢ (ΔG° ≈ −30 kJ/mol) to drive reactions that would not go alone. You can also compute ΔG° = ΣnΔG°f(products) − ΣnΔG°f(reactants).

      Check yourself: ΔH > 0 and ΔS > 0. When is the process favorable?

      AP Unit 9

      Galvanic cells & cell potential

      A battery is a chemical reaction pulled apart so its electrons have to travel through a wire. The voltage is how hard they are being pushed.

      The idea

      Put a zinc strip in copper(II) sulfate solution and the zinc dissolves while copper plates out: electrons hop directly from Zn to Cu²⁺. Now separate the two halves: zinc in one beaker, copper in another, joined by a wire. The electrons can't hop, so they flow through the wire. That flow is electricity, and you can run a light bulb on it. This is a galvanic (voltaic) cell.

      The electrode where oxidation happens is the anode (it loses electrons); where reduction happens is the cathode. Mnemonic: An Ox and Red Cat. Electrons flow from anode to cathode through the wire. A salt bridge lets ions drift between the beakers to keep each solution neutral: anions toward the anode, cations toward the cathode. The cell's voltage is E°cell = E°cathode − E°anode, using standard reduction potentials. A positive E° means the reaction is spontaneous.

      Assumption upgrade Before, the standard potential assumed 1 M solutions at 25 °C. Real cells aren't: concentrations change as the cell runs. The Nernst equation corrects for that: E = E° − (0.0592/n) log Q. As reactants are used up Q rises toward K, and the voltage falls to zero: a "dead" battery is a cell at equilibrium.
      Cell potentialE°cell = E°cathode − E°anode
      Free energyΔG° = −nFE°F = 96 485 C/mol e⁻
      Nernst (25 °C)E = E° − (0.0592/n) log QE° = (0.0592/n) log K
      Build a battery
      E°cell—
      E (now)—
      Anode (oxidation)—
      Cathode (reduction)—
      Q—
      n (electrons)—
      ΔG°—
      K—

      Try this

      Predict the anode and the voltage, then check.

      1. Zinc on the left, copper on the right. Which is the anode? What is E°cell?

        What you should see

        Zinc is the anode (oxidized: it has the lower reduction potential, −0.76 V) and copper the cathode (+0.34 V). E°cell = 0.34 − (−0.76) = 1.10 V.

      2. Press Run the cell. What happens to the voltage as the cell runs down?

        What you should see

        It slowly falls: [Zn²⁺] rises and [Cu²⁺] falls, so Q rises. When Q = K the voltage reaches 0 V and the battery is dead. (K is about 10³⁷ for this cell, so it runs a long time.)

      3. Use the same metal on both sides but make one solution 100 times more dilute.

        What you should see

        A concentration cell: E° is 0 V, yet the cell still produces about 0.059 V. The dilute side is the anode (copper dissolves there, raising its concentration) and the concentrated side is the cathode.

      Worked example

      A cell is made from Zn(s) | Zn²⁺(0.010 M) and Cu²⁺(1.0 M) | Cu(s). Standard potentials: Cu²⁺/Cu = +0.34 V, Zn²⁺/Zn = −0.76 V. Find E°cell, then E, then ΔG°.

      Try it yourself first, then reveal one step at a time.

      1. Anode and cathode. The metal with the lower reduction potential is oxidized: Zn is the anode, Cu the cathode. Reaction: Zn + Cu²⁺ → Zn²⁺ + Cu, n = 2.
      2. Standard potential. E°cell = E°(cathode) − E°(anode) = 0.34 − (−0.76) = +1.10 V.
      3. Nernst. Q = [Zn²⁺]/[Cu²⁺] = 0.010/1.0 = 0.010. E = 1.10 − (0.0592/2) log(0.010) = 1.10 + 0.0592 = 1.16 V. (Less product than standard, so a bit more voltage.)
      4. Free energy. ΔG° = −nFE° = −(2)(96485)(1.10) = −212 000 J = −212 kJ per mole of reaction. Negative, matching the positive E°.

      Common mistakes

      • Flipping the sign of E° when you multiply the half-reaction by a coefficient. Potentials are intensive: they do not change when you double the equation (but n does).
      • Subtracting in the wrong order: E°cell = E°cathode − E°anode, with both as reduction potentials.
      • Mixing up the direction of electron flow (anode → cathode) with conventional current, and anions/cations in the salt bridge.
      • Forgetting the sign convention for Q in Nernst: Q has products over reactants, and pure solids are left out.
      • Calling a negative E° "no reaction". It means the reverse reaction is the spontaneous one.

      Connections

      E°, ΔG° and K are three views of the same fact. Positive E° ⇔ negative ΔG° ⇔ K > 1. At equilibrium (a dead cell), E = 0 and Q = K. Batteries (alkaline, lithium-ion, lead-acid) are galvanic cells designed so that the cell potential stays close to constant while they discharge, and rechargeable ones are run backwards as electrolytic cells.

      Check yourself: in the external wire of a galvanic cell, electrons flow…

      AP Unit 9

      Electrolysis & Faraday's law

      Run a battery backwards: push electrons through a cell with an outside power supply and force a reaction that wouldn't happen by itself.

      The idea

      A galvanic cell is a ball rolling downhill and giving you work. An electrolytic cell is the opposite: you use an outside power supply to push the ball uphill. The reaction has a negative E° (not spontaneous), so you must apply more voltage than |E°| to make it go. This is how aluminum, chlorine and sodium hydroxide are made, how metals are refined and plated, and how a rechargeable battery recharges.

      The definitions don't change: oxidation at the anode, reduction at the cathode (An Ox, Red Cat). What flips is the sign: in an electrolytic cell the cathode is wired to the negative terminal of the supply (it is where electrons are pushed in) and the anode to the positive terminal. Faraday's law counts the product: every mole of electrons (96 485 C) deposits 1/z mole of a metal ion of charge z⁺. The amount = (current × time) ÷ (F × z).

      Assumption upgrade Before, we only used cells that run on their own. Now we force reactions with electricity, so in aqueous solutions water competes: it can be reduced at the cathode (making H₂) or oxidized at the anode (making O₂). Whichever reaction needs the least voltage happens first.
      Chargeq = I × tcoulombs = amperes × seconds
      Moles of e⁻n(e⁻) = q / FF = 96 485 C/mol
      Moles of productn = n(e⁻) / zz = electrons per atom or per molecule
      Electroplate a metal
      Charge passed—
      Moles of e⁻—
      Moles of metal—
      Mass plated—
      What forms at each electrode?

      Cathode (reduction)—
      Anode (oxidation)—
      Minimum voltage—
      Status—

      Try this

      Predict the products first.

      1. Double the current. Does it plate twice as much in the same time?

        What you should see

        Yes: charge = I × t, so twice the current moves twice the electrons and deposits twice the mass. About 3.6 g of copper after 30 min at 6.00 A.

      2. Plate silver and copper with the same current and time. Which gives more mass?

        What you should see

        Silver: each Ag⁺ needs only one electron (z = 1) and an Ag atom is heavier (107.9 g/mol), so the same charge (5400 C at 3.00 A for 30 min) deposits 6.0 g of silver but only 1.8 g of copper (z = 2, 63.55 g/mol): about 3.4 times as much.

      3. Electrolyze aqueous sodium sulfate. Which ions react?

        What you should see

        Neither Na⁺ nor SO₄²⁻: water is reduced at the cathode (H₂) and oxidized at the anode (O₂). Na⁺ is too hard to reduce in water and sulfate is already fully oxidized. The net result is water splitting.

      Worked example

      A current of 2.50 A flows for 45.0 minutes through a solution of Cu²⁺. What mass of copper plates onto the cathode? (M = 63.55 g/mol, F = 96 485 C/mol)

      Try it yourself first, then reveal one step at a time.

      1. Charge. t = 45.0 min × 60 = 2700 s. q = I t = (2.50 A)(2700 s) = 6750 C.
      2. Moles of electrons. n(e⁻) = 6750 / 96485 = 0.06996 mol.
      3. Moles of copper. Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu, so n(Cu) = 0.06996 / 2 = 0.03498 mol.
      4. Mass. 0.03498 mol × 63.55 g/mol = 2.22 g of copper.

      Common mistakes

      • Forgetting to convert minutes or hours to seconds before multiplying by amperes.
      • Forgetting z: Cu²⁺ needs 2 electrons per atom, Al³⁺ needs 3.
      • Giving the cathode a "+" sign in an electrolytic cell. It is negative here (but still the site of reduction).
      • Predicting that Na or K metal forms from an aqueous solution. Water is reduced first, giving H₂.
      • Forgetting that applied voltage must exceed |E°cell| (and real cells need extra for overpotential).

      Galvanic vs electrolytic

      Galvanic: spontaneous (E° > 0), produces electricity, anode is −, cathode is +. Electrolytic: non-spontaneous (E° < 0), consumes electricity, anode is +, cathode is −. In both, oxidation is at the anode, reduction at the cathode, and electrons flow anode → cathode through the wire (the power supply pushes them in the electrolytic case).

      Check yourself: how many moles of electrons pass when 2.00 A flows for 1.00 hour?

      Which tool do I use?

      Most of the time lost on the exam goes into choosing a method. Learn the clues, then practice picking.

      The intuition

      Each problem type leaves clues. Words like "how many grams" point to a mole-ratio road. "At equilibrium" means K and an ICE table. A solution that contains both a weak acid and its conjugate base means a buffer. Name the road first; the arithmetic is the easy part.

      Exam review

      Build a mixed problem set from the units your exam covers. No hints during the set; everything is graded and explained when you submit.

      Exam format

      AP Chemistry · May 2027 exam · 3 hours 15 minutes total

      Section I: Multiple choice
      60 questions · 90 min · 50%
      Four answer choices each. Many come in sets built around one graph, table or particle diagram. About 1.5 minutes per question.
      Section II: Free response
      7 questions · 105 min · 50%
      • 3 long questions, about 10 points each (roughly 20 minutes apiece)
      • 4 short questions, about 4 points each (roughly 9 minutes apiece)
      Expect lab design, data analysis, particle drawings and multi-step calculations.
      How you take it
      Hybrid digital. You answer multiple choice in the Bluebook app. Free-response questions appear in Bluebook, and you handwrite your answers in a paper booklet.
      Calculator
      Allowed on both sections: an approved scientific or graphing calculator, or the Desmos calculator built into Bluebook.
      Reference sheet
      A periodic table and an equations and constants sheet are provided. This site's Reference button has a similar sheet.

      Review my mistakes

      Every problem you miss in the practice set or exam review lands here and comes back with new numbers. Spacing reviews out over days is one of the most reliable ways to make things stick.

      How the queue works

      Miss a problem: it's due right away. Get it right: it comes back in 1 day, then 3 days, then 7. After three correct reviews in a row it's mastered and leaves the queue. Miss it again and the count restarts.
